This book is a crime thriller but is more than that!! Human Psychology, child psychology, love, betrayal, murder, foolproof crime planning, and a lot more.

Book Starts with Amy- The female protagonist, missing from her house on the day of her fifth marriage Anniversary. The crime scene looks like a kidnapping case. When the police investigation starts, all clues evidence point to Nick- her Husband & male protagonist of the Story. Every year Amy used to set up a treasure hunt for Nick for his Anniversary Gift. This year was the same, but while searching for the treasure hunt, Nick found something that changed the whole perception of the story.

In the first part of the story, things might seem clear, the story might seem boring and you feel you know the murderer. But wait till you reach the second part, there is an unexpected twist! And you would be wandering about the patience in planning and plotting things. You would be reading Amy and Nick’s side of the story simultaneously. This was a long read, but yeah one of the kind, you can’t put down to get quickly to the end, especially after the first part. On some pages it was boring but overall it’s a gripping Mystery Book. But I am a little disappointed with the end of the Book. I was expecting to have some better Ending.

His character simply shows not to underestimate even a common man. The Man who brings the whole Bharat under one kingdom unified. Who gave India its powerful Emperor Chandragupta Maurya. & no wonder we still refer to ‘Chanakya Neeti’ in politics. A simple Brahmin Scholar who made his life goal to ‘unite Bharat’ either by hook or crook.

Chanakya’s Chant is written by Ashwin Sanghi, who is known for his Mythological Fiction Writings. No doubt the author has a deep knowledge of Indian history which will be visible throughout the Book. Writer narrated two different periods side by side. one chapter taking you to the Era of Chanakaya and the next bringing you to the modern political Era.

What Binds both Eras together is the Lead character of Story ‘Ganga prasad Mishra’- a simple brahmin History teacher from Kanpur who landed accidentally in the ruins of great Man ad Emperor & got something valuable which shaped his future. And never a fair Game even if you r working for good.

It’s quite a Gripping novel, but maybe at some point, you might feel it boring with political facts & figures and all but overall it’s a good read. It would be a new kind of experience to read two different stories of two different Eras side by side. It took me a little longer to finish the book but quite impressed by the work of the author on little details.

There are a few male authors who have this unique power of writing down females emotions so beautifully that you might wonder is it work of a male author or a female has poured out her heart.

I remember I came across author’s facebook page’s some post & I instantly fell in love with the lines. I started following the page and I realised those all post are part of the book. So one fine day I just picked the book to give a try and I was totally in awe with the words, with the emotions, with the message it conveys. It was totally like someone has written what I exactly feel as a woman.

Reflection of A Man is beautifully written by Mr. Amari Soul . Many of us have been into toxicity without even knowing that we are into one. Reflection of A Man simply says how a man should be in a relationship, how he needs to treat her lady. Because knowing a female’s emotions is not complicated but we make it so. On the Other for female, it is trying to let them know if they are in a toxic relationship, with the person who doesn’t give them what they deserve. If it’s the time to get out of toxicity believing in the strong woman that she is.

It’s an attempt by the author to make women self-aware, more powerful, and more understanding about what a healthy relationship looks like, what they ask from their partner is not too much. So I would say whether you are a male or a female, both should read this book once. It would surely be a page-turner in a relationship. So you know kind of win-win situation for both male and Female. Make sure you bring positive changes to your partner’s life.

Book is mainly focused on enhancing the quality of relationship between a male and female, be it married couples or girlfriend boyfriend. It is gonna be a good read for both male and female as the writer tried his best to write down the both parts.

Title: The Modern Break-Up

Personal notes:
Being a millennial, I could relate to the fact that Dating and relationships have lost their charm in Modern World. We are now looking for our Love on dating Apps randomly swiping the profiles. Sometimes it starts with a spark but that so-called spark fades away quickly. Sometimes the other person ghosts us or sometimes we simply lose interest in the individual. The person we want, in turn, want someone else, and those who want us we don’t want them, and this cycle goes on. Complicated Right?

In the world of this Social Media and the Internet, Our way of dealing with Breakups have also changed. Breakup followed by late-night stalking, checking their last seen, typing a long emotional message, but then in conflict whether to send them or not. Whether these efforts would bring the Person back? I believe- No, it won’t. It would make you more miserable. I won’t say breakup and moving on is easy but knowing self-worth and moving on is much better right? Rather than continuously thinking what went wrong and questioning your own value.

Well coming to the Book, The Modern Breakup wonderfully written by Daniel Chidiac. Initially may be you would find the book a little boring but once you would get in to the rhythm of reading, trust me you would relate to each and every word as millennial or I should say person like me stuck in modern day Dating. What make this Book Unique? Either you are Male or a Female, both would relate to it because usually either it’s about male or female. But here author Balanced both sides so well.

As a Female, I feel sometimes that Men Find it easy to go for casual/ hookups thing. And having male friends I know they somewhere feel the same. But guess what we are emotionally exhausted after investing our time & energy on someone who doesn’t deserve it. So if you are a millennial you would relate to it while reading the book, and if you are not like one of us you would surely say, what this generation has got itself into.

Well but the book surely deserves one Reading, I promise you won’t regret investing time in it, at least I don’t. Get your copy and face the truth, you would learn a lot with this book especially about yourself, another gender, and of course dating & relationships. One last piece of advice from my side for Dating in modern Days – “Be clear about your intentions from the very beginning with the other person- you want casual say it, you want a hookup to say it, you want relationship make it clear, you want a commitment tell them. JUST BE CLEAR to save yourself from complications”

I have seen foreigners coming to India for their researches in neuroscience because they think India has answers to all the questions that they are searching for. I have seen foreigners being devotees of ‘Krishna’, I have seen them reading ‘Geeta’ and adopting it in their way of living. And trust me it’s a matter of pride to know this, we are part of a country that is only one of its kind.

Apprenticed to a Himalayan Master -The Autobiography of ‘Shri M’, is surely an inspiring and amazing journey of A Muslim boy attracted by Vedas & Upanishads philosophy and attracted by the Secrets of Spirituality hidden in snow-capped mountains of Himalayas. Book is not only his journey to be a great yogi but it is a good chance to know the rich culture of India, to know the true meaning of religions, to know the country you live in from a different view. I was completely astonished while reading the book finding out that the great Spiritual Souls don’t have any grudges on religion! They all r one and bless you if you’re a true seeker!

Also, the book gave a wonderful view of India’s diverse religious culture and the beauty of souls who chose India as their place! From mountains to beaches from deserts to plateau India holds the power to attract even foreigners to resides in India and adopt our ancient way of living. From the Sufi souls to great yogis to great philanthropists to lamas you would find great souls making India their home & making its global power in spirituality and yogic powers!

Also, books explain to you the true beauty of the Himalayas and Uttarakhand. The book is worth reading if you are mesmerized by Indian and Himalayas Beauty & Spirituality! We all know the importance of the Himalayas- being the abode of Shivji and many great sages. Himalaya is not beautiful in terms of view but it is also important as it is home to so many Great Souls, so many herbal plants and medicine, and hides deep secrets inside. The beauty of the Himalayas is mesmerizing so is its spiritual importance.

Those who think India doesn’t have much to offer in comparison to developed countries, I would proudly tell them that people from those developed countries live in India as yogis adapting Indian culture! Those who debate on the religions I would surely recommend this book to them, I m pretty sure their thoughts would change as if you know the core of any religion they all believed in humanity, and all r one !!!
I m happy I came across this book and it surely gave me so many reasons to Love India and be a proud Indian!!!

So go grab your copy if you are mesmerized by the beauty of the Himalayas if you also want to know more about ‘India’ and its rich cultural heritage.

A hundred little lamps – this not your usual Romance Fiction novel, it’s way beyond that. When I picked this book I had no idea what it holds. And trust me it’s a new experience. The book is about the true bond between a grandson and a grandfather. It’s about a grandson who becomes his grandfather’s secret holder in some weeks. It’s about their endless conversations, it’s about their love, it’s about the conversation between two generations. It’s about a grandson’s effort to save his grandfather from his own Son. It’s about a grandson’s endeavor to find his grandfather’s old love and bring them together despite society.

It’s about a father who tried his best to give the best to his kids, to give them happiness, to educate them, make them capable of differentiating between wrong and right. But when he did something that makes him happy, his kids humiliated him and pointed him wrong. It’s about a father betrayed by his son, just because he looked for companionship in his old days.

It was not the love holding lust, it was pure form were spending time matters, where the happiness matters, where seeing the other smile matters, where respect for each other matters, where the spark of love never dies. Where the intimacy was emotional not the physical. What’s wrong if two people understand each other and just be themselves? Why we as a society can’t accept the fact that loves is not always about getting involved physically, it’s way beyond that?

As I read the book it was a new Experience, to read about the old-time love stories. They are not like modern age relationships. And this book surely shows a beautiful story. This book is an example of how beautifully two generations learn from each other. The author did a really good job in writing so beautifully that I was able to visualize each moment in my mind. And as I always say this is the beauty of an Author and makes it a bestseller…

Title: A Thousand Splendid Suns
Author: Khaled Hosseini

One-line recommendation: A heart-wrenching and thought-provoking novel that explores the resilience of women in the face of war, patriarchy, and oppression.
Personal notes:
When I started the book I had no idea the book will end like this. The book has so much in it- life in war, women’s rights, women’s condition in olden times, patriarchy, love, betrayal, innocence so many emotions so many characters. And trust me this book will bind you till the end.

A Thousand Splendid Suns- by Khaled Hosseini. This is my first read of Khaled Hosseini but I am awestruck with his magic of words. From the beginning till the end of the novel you would feel like you are witnessing the whole Story as being a part of it. You could visualize every scene, every emotion. And that’s what I love about a writer his power of imagination and the power of imagination he gives to his readers while reading the book.

The story is set in Afghanistan and the beautiful city of “Kabul” during the time the forty-year span in war-torn Afghanistan – from before the Communist era through civil war, the Taliban, and the arrival of American troops. This is the story about Two Ladies whose Fate takes them together. Story of endless domestic abuses, story of motherhood, the story of not giving up to life, the story of survival, suffering, and sacrifice.

So the Story starts with a little girl- Mariam, who doesn’t even know the meaning of “Harami”. Her life is confined to the periphery of his little home because she is illegitimate for the outer world. At age of 14 when we barely know how to take care of ourselves, she lost her mother, her father married her off to a man much older than her. She has no right over her life, over her decisions. When a girl gets married she has so many dreams but her dreams are shattered one by one. For her husband, she was just a means of having a Son and fulfill his physical needs. Sadly even Decades later there are still people like this for whom women are just machines to have kids and Complete physical needs.

Laila- another protagonist of the story lost her wife in the war violence, got married to the old man for the sake of a kid in her womb. It’s strange how much sacrifice a mother does for her kid. The story is about women and their losing self-worth. But it’s said that everything has a limit and one day that limit crosses and you have to either do or die. The decision is hard but eventually the end of the suffering.

I will be honest there was a mixture of emotions that I am not able to pen down in straight. But yes it was an emotional read. It was heartbreaking to read women clad in Burkha, banned from studies and freedom. Women enduring years of domestic violence but never uttering a word because of no court for them. I admire the dareness of both ladies who survived each day and keep on being each other’s strength.

So I would say yes the book is worth reading. It’s not your one-sitting book but it’s worth the time. You would feel like your just witnessing all these incidents standing right there and feeling their emotions.

I randomly picked that book on the weekend & With easy language and storyline, I was able to finish it in one sitting. What made me stick to the book was the way the author explained the beauty of relations. Book focused on a lot of points like domestic violence, marriage, love, family bonding, a brother’s love for their sister, a mother’s love for her newborn daughter. So it was a book that makes you experience different forms of love at once.

This is the story of A girl married to a man with so many dreams but ended up facing domestic violence. This is the story of a brother going all the lengths to save her sister and give her the best of life. This is the story of a cousin who wished, the world to know the story of her cousin and let the world know about her, helping others ladies like her to make their own choice and put an end to the violence they are facing for ages.

Book touched on the very susceptible topic of Indian society- marriage and Domestic violence. Hundreds of married females face this one way or another but never dare to say a word. They endure it because that’s what they have been teaching! But it’s time to stop this and let the male Dominant Society knows that we as females are not going to tolerate this now. I admire the courage with which Adya left her in-law’s house. I admire the way her family supported her decision. I admire the way her brother made it his responsibility to protect her sister and newborn niece. I admire the way her cousin Arjun, always been there for her unconditionally, giving many of us serious sibling and cousin goals.

We all love our family, but we rarely express our love to them. Never tell them what they meant to us. That’s how a brother-sister relationship is right? They fight but they protect each other unconditionally. The book is more about the message that it’s never too late to start fresh. It’s just a matter of time to decide if we want to face this or keep suffering. For me it’s was an emotional read, because being the eldest kid of a family I always want to protect my family at any cost. One more reason for reading this book was the way Agastya taking care of her sister during pregnancy and reading books on how to take care of her niece. That melted my heart ￼

So as for the book, if you are looking for some easy language, lite read; please go for it, you won’t be disappointed. Even for beginners, this could be a good read. This is not a love story but a life story of people finally making it to sunny days ￼

“The Mahabharata Secret by Christopher C. Doyle”– a book that kept me glued to it from beginning till end. Every writer is good in itself but I feel the mytho fictional writers do an exceptional job when they connect the present world to the centuries-old events and take their reader on an adventure journey in History. And I don’t need to say that Cristopher C. Doyle is one of those Authors. I was able to visualise every event in my mind whether present or past. He was able to maintain the suspense throughout the book that With every page ending I want to read more & more. & This is the power that makes you a good Writer.

So Book is the Journey of finding a Secret related to the Mahabharata Era which could turn out to be a disaster to the world. The story is set in India and the regions coving the Gupta Dynasty’s Empire in ancient times. A secret that when discovered by wrong people could destroy Mankind. The book is written in Three-time frames- King Ashoka’s Time, the present day, and Mahabharata Era. A young man along with his friend set to solve a puzzle e-mailed by his Uncle before his Mysterious death, without even realizing what they getting into.

It is said Ashoka Founded a Secret Brotherhood Society to protect the Secret after the secret was discovered by one of his courtiers. The Story is based on the same. Well, I don’t know if that’s just fiction or any truth behind it, but one thing I know is this book was one hell of an adventurous Ride. With the Terrorist organizations, international business tycoons, politicans, and many other trying to get their hands on the secret hidden from hundreds of years, this was a gripping experience.

For me, this was the no Doubt worth the read. With interest in Indian history, Mythology, military operations, and suspense book, this book was a complete package of all. Without a second thought, I would recommend anyone to read it. My thoughts still drift to this book, even though I have completed it three days. One-line recommendation: A haunting and thought-provoking novel that explores the complexities of human relationships, guilt, and redemption, set against the backdrop of war-torn Afghanistan.
Personal notes:
Reading the books like “The Kite Runner” might leave you with depressing emotions but they would surely make you ponder over many thoughts. I had finished the book some weeks back but It took me time to write this. There so so many emotions I felt while reading the book then I wasn’t able to phrase them into words. When a happy childhood turns into your worst regret that haunts you for the whole of life because your gut feeling knows you were wrong at that point.

The story starts when Afghanistan used to be a happy beautiful country where people live in happiness and peace, but a Major part of the Story sets in the War days of Aghanistan which is still under War situation. It is about the childhood of Two Kids who grow up together more like brothers but never knew the biggest truth of their life. I won’t say it’s a ‘happy ever after’ story because it is not. But sometimes you need to feel another side of emotions as well. Those depressing, heartbreaking, scary emotions. Imagine living in the country under the constant threat of the Taliban? Scary no?

Hassan and Amir- the names around which this story revolves. Those who have read the book might feel bad for Hassan, but I equally feel bad for Amir. Because his actions even though not justified, were more of the result of the insecurities raised by his father. And as a kid I guess we want our parent’s undivided love and it makes us cross our limit. So does Amir, but he had that regret for life. Hasan on the other end, I feel was the purest soul, who was so selfless, but just suffered for most of life. Just imagine getting raped at a little age? And still, braving a smile as nothing happened? Could you think of the state of that kid? It’s scary even to think!

But we all get a chance to repay for our mistakes so does Amir, rescuing his son of Hassan. But the kid shared the same fate as his father’s childhood. I don’t think it’s easy to get over the trauma of childhood events but it scares me even to imagine the situation when a kid doesn’t have parents, no house, no family to go to. While reading the book I was hoping it to be a happy ending but the book ends in uncertainty.

Reading this book generates a curiosity in me to know the current situation in Afghanistan, and I end up talking to an Afghan Friend about the same. And it’s heartbreaking to know they are still in war, still under the threat of Taliban’s and terrorism, who don’t have mercy word in their dictionary. They just know killing people, shedding blood in the name of Allah. And I m pretty sure these guys never have read the Quran once else they won’t have been this barbaric.

Well, some emotions you feel are really strong especially the tragic ones and make you think deep. I don’t know if you would want to experience the journey of Amir and Hassan, and the Life Aghan people are having. But yes I would say one thing this book will give you a never-before experience.

This is the story of the ‘Marsh girl’ who stands firm against the world, who didn’t care about the judgments. Who knows how to protect herself from evil people. She proved she is intelligent of all and will never comprise with her dignity and self-respect even if it cost a life.

The book keeps you hooked till the end, though initially, it might get boring, you won’t be disappointed. It’s worth the patience. It’s one of the amazing books have come across.

How kya survive alone? Why did her family left her one by one? How could she write books when she never went to school? How she learnt to earn? How did she get vast knowledge of marsh? "A Thousand Ships" is brutally honest and profoundly moving. Haynes masterfully narrates the stories of these women, bringing their suffering and resilience to light. Amid the loneliness of her remote existence, Circe grows as she navigates complex encounters with both mortals and gods. Through Miller’s empathetic storytelling, Circe’s journey of self-discovery unfolds, transforming her into a character of profound resilience and complexity.

One of the book’s greatest strengths is Miller’s unique and modernized perspective on Circe’s myth. The author goes beyond traditional portrayals to develop Circe as a nuanced, layered figure who grows from a misunderstood, isolated child to a powerful and self-aware woman. Miller’s narrative style adds a contemporary voice to Circe’s ancient world, drawing readers into her struggles, emotional depth, and moments of self-realization in a way that feels strikingly relevant.

✨
In conclusion, Circe is a beautifully crafted and immersive reimagining of Greek mythology, ideal for anyone who enjoys myth retellings with powerful, introspective characters. The author’s storytelling draws readers into a fascinating multiverse where divine and earthly realms intertwine.

Part Two takes a different approach, focusing on nine stories that highlight the often-overlooked qualities of Mahadevi within ordinary women of today. These stories, many based on real-life events, shed light on the subtle yet powerful strength and divinity that women embody in their everyday lives.

What makes *Mahadevi* stand out is Kaintura’s ability to marry ancient myths with modern sensibilities. The writing style is engaging, making complex philosophical and spiritual ideas accessible to all readers. The book highlights the resilience and spiritual depth of women, presenting them as the living embodiments of divine energy.

This book offers a unique and insightful exploration of Hindu mythology, and it does so in a way that challenges conventional perceptions. *Mahadevi* is an excellent read for those looking to dive deeper into the concepts of womanhood, mythology, and divine power. Book Review: Trishul by Paranay Bhalerao

The final installment of the Kavach Trilogy, Trishul, by Paranay Bhalerao, is a thrilling conclusion to a saga blending mythology and fiction. With a gripping narrative that spans across timelines, the book takes readers on a journey filled with prophecy, power, and the eternal clash of Dharma and Adharma.

The story revolves around Shaurya’s relentless quest for Lord Shiva’s ultimate weapon, the Trishul, while the prophecy about the Kavach—"The one who breaks the Kavach must die"—adds a layer of tension. As Shaurya and Rudra take the spotlight with their intense conflict, Teena’s transformation and her path of vengeance bring emotional depth to the narrative.

Bhalerao’s storytelling is exceptional. The seamless shifts between 555 BCE and the present day, combined with vivid descriptions of settings like Konark and the Himalayan mountains, make for an immersive experience. The narrative's balance of mythological lore and modern-day intrigue keeps the reader hooked throughout.

However, I found Isha’s storyline a bit underwhelming. Compared to the high-stakes arcs of Shaurya and Rudra, her character felt sidelined, and her presence did not add much to the central plot, leaving a loose end in an otherwise tightly woven story.

Despite this, Trishul is a remarkable read. The author’s ability to blend ancient myths, like the Kavach of Karna, with modern storytelling is commendable. Each twist keeps the tension alive, and the characters’ struggles feel genuine and relatable.

Highly recommended for fans of mythological fiction, Trishul is a fitting finale to the Kavach Trilogy. Paranay Bhalerao delivers a tale that lingers in your mind, making it a must-read for anyone who enjoys a blend of mythology and suspense.

Set in Nazi Germany during World War II, "The Book Thief" is a deeply moving story narrated by Death itself. It follows Liesel Meminger, a young girl sent to live with foster parents in a small town near Munich. As she struggles to adapt to her new life, she finds solace in books—some stolen, some gifted—and in the unbreakable bonds she forms with those around her.

This book had been on my TBR for so long, but I was hesitant to pick it up. It wasn’t until my friend insisted that I finally did—and I’m so glad they did. Initially, I found myself confused as the story took time to settle, but once it did, I was completely engrossed.

"The Book Thief" is one of the most heartbreaking books I’ve ever read. By the time I reached the final pages, I was in tears. The last scene, set after the bombing, shattered me into pieces. And that one moment—when Liesel kisses Rudy—was utterly devastating.

Beyond its emotional weight, what makes this book truly unforgettable is its beautifully poetic writing and deeply human characters. My favorite was Liesel’s foster father, Hans Hubermann—his patience, kindness, and unwavering support for her during her nightmares made my heart ache in the best way. And the innocent, playful friendship between Liesel and Rudy was just as precious.

Despite the heartbreak, I would recommend "The Book Thief" to everyone. It’s a story that lingers, a reminder of the power of words, love, and resilience even in the darkest times.

Personal notes:
For our book club *Fates & Fabes*, we chose *Stone Blind* by Natalie Haynes as our March read, aligning with Women’s History Month. Medusa is one of the most misunderstood figures in mythology, and I was eager to see her story from a fresh perspective. However, while the book was a compelling read, I found myself wanting more of Medusa’s voice.

Rather than being solely focused on Medusa, *Stone Blind* weaves together multiple narratives—gods, mortals, and creatures—all giving their version of events. While this added depth to the story, it also diluted Medusa’s presence. I had hoped for a stronger, more personal account of her experiences, but she often felt lost among the many perspectives. That said, the author’s storytelling was captivating. Natalie Haynes has a way of making ancient myths feel modern, questioning long-held beliefs, and challenging our understanding of who the real monsters are.

One of the most thought-provoking aspects of this book was its portrayal of the Greek gods. It reinforced something I’ve often felt—these so-called divine beings are far from noble. Instead, they are driven by selfish desires, lust, jealousy, and vengeance, often inflicting suffering on mortals just because they can. Their actions make them seem worse than the humans they rule over. This book highlighted how myths have long justified cruelty, especially towards women, under the guise of divine will.

Despite my wish for a more Medusa-centric narrative, I appreciated how *Stone Blind* challenged the traditional villainization of her character. It made me question how many “monsters” in history were simply victims of those in power.

Title: A House Without Windows
Author: Nadia Hashimi
Themes: grief; identity; resilience; patriarchy; mother-daughter relationships

One-line recommendation: A heart-wrenching and thought-provoking exploration of women's resilience in the face of patriarchal oppression.
Personal notes:
After reading *Sparks Like Stars*, this is my third book by Nadia Hashimi, and I can confidently say she is now an auto-buy author for me. Her storytelling has a way of immersing you in the lives of Afghan women, bringing to light their struggles, resilience, and unbreakable spirit.

We picked this book as our 'Chapter Chatters' Bookclub's March BOTM resonating with the March being Women in history month. Set in Afghanistan, *The House Without Windows* tells the heartbreaking yet powerful story of Zeba, a woman imprisoned for a crime against her husband. But she is not alone—her story echoes those of countless women in Chil Mehtab, a prison filled with others who have been condemned not for their actions, but for daring to survive in a society that punishes them for defending themselves.

One of the most compelling aspects of this book was the narration. While Zeba’s journey is central, her mother truly stole the limelight, emerging as a fierce and strong-willed woman from the very beginning. Her presence in the story was powerful, shaping Zeba’s own resilience. And then there’s Basir—Zeba’s son—whose maturity and unwavering support for his mother made him one of the most admirable characters. Despite everything, he stood by her, embodying strength beyond his years.

The book is deeply emotional, making you question the injustice women face and the way their lives are dictated by patriarchal norms. Yet, what I love most about Nadia Hashimi’s books is that they always end on a hopeful note. After all the pain and struggle, the story leaves you with the belief that change is possible—that someday, women in Afghanistan will live with the freedom they deserve.

This book was heartbreaking yet uplifting, filled with powerful moments of love, sacrifice, and resilience. If you haven’t read Nadia Hashimi yet, I highly recommend picking up her books. They stay with you long after you’ve turned the last page.

*Koral Das Gupta’s Sati Series* has been an absolute delight to read, and *Mandodari* was no exception. This was my fourth book in the series, and with every installment, I find myself completely engrossed in the powerful narratives of mythology’s often-overlooked women.

Told from Mandodari’s perspective, this book offers a fresh and compelling take on the woman who stood beside Raavan—the great king, the feared warrior, and the deeply flawed man. What sets this story apart is how Mandodari is not just portrayed as Raavan’s wife but as an individual with her own strengths, intellect, and emotions. She is defined by her brilliance as an architect, a skill she inherited from her father, but she is also a woman who struggles between duty and personal anguish.

Throughout the book, we witness Mandodari’s journey—her love, her pain, and the burden of being married to a man who was both powerful and self-destructive. She sees his greatness but also his downfall, and the emotional turmoil she endures is deeply moving. Unlike the typical portrayal of Raavan as just a villain, this book gives a nuanced view of their relationship—one filled with admiration, frustration, and heartbreak.

As always, Koral Das Gupta’s writing is mesmerizing. She has a way of breathing life into mythology’s female protagonists, making their stories impossible to put down. Her storytelling is immersive, her prose flows beautifully, and she makes you crave more even after the last page is turned.

This was a refreshing and thought-provoking read, shedding light on a woman often overshadowed in the grand narratives of the Ramayana. Highly recommended for anyone who loves mythology, especially stories that reclaim the voices of strong yet forgotten women.

Title: Babel
Author: R.F. Kuang

One-line recommendation: A stunning and ambitious novel that will make you think about the power of language and the weight of history.
Personal notes:
This book had been on my TBR for so long—partly because of its stunning aesthetic cover and partly because of the glowing reviews. Finally, thanks to my friend for gifting me a copy and convincing me to pick it up!

I’ll admit, I’m not usually a fan of classics or dense literary fiction, and at first, *Babel* felt a bit slow with its deep dive into grammar and etymology. But once the magic of silver and translation came into play, I was completely hooked. The way R.F. Kuang intertwined language, colonialism, and power was nothing short of brilliant. It made me think about how words shape our world and who gets to control their meaning.

As for the characters, I truly enjoyed the dynamic between Robin and Rafi. Their friendship, their adventures, and the camaraderie they shared made the book all the more engaging. So, when the ending came… let’s just say, I was *not* ready. I didn’t know what I was expecting, but definitely not *that*! The emotional weight of their deaths hit hard, leaving a sense of devastation that lingered long after I turned the last page.

Would I recommend *Babel*? Absolutely. It’s a deeply intellectual, thought-provoking, and ambitious novel. But would I reread it? Probably not. It took me weeks to finish, and while I loved the experience, it’s not the kind of book I’d revisit soon. The writing style, though, was phenomenal—R.F. Kuang’s meticulous research on language and grammatica was evident on every page, and I truly appreciated the depth she brought to the story.

Overall, *Babel* was a unique reading experience, blending fantasy, history, and linguistics in a way I’ve never seen before. While it may not be a book I’ll revisit, I’m definitely intrigued to pick up more from the author in the future.

Personal notes:
Elif Shafak has cemented herself as my auto-buy author, and this book once again reminded me why. The way she seamlessly blends mythology with history and the present is nothing short of mesmerizing. Her storytelling pulls you in, making the past feel alive and the present feel like a continuation of something much older.

This book takes the journey of a single drop of water, flowing from ancient Mesopotamian times to modern-day London, tracing its impact across different civilizations. At first, I found it a bit disorienting—three timelines, three different lives, all interwoven—but as I kept reading, the pieces started falling into place. The storytelling mirrors the movement of water itself—sometimes still, sometimes turbulent, but always finding its way.

What truly stood out for me was Shafak’s ability to make history feel tangible. Her descriptions of places and eras were so vivid that I wanted to visit the ruins of Nineveh, to stand before the grand Lamassu statues she described so poetically. She makes you feel the weight of time, the importance of heritage, and the unseen threads that connect people across centuries.

The characters added such emotional depth to the narrative. Narin’s story, in particular, stayed with me—the resilience, the pain, the quiet strength. Zaleekhah’s journey of heartbreak and rediscovery felt incredibly raw and real. And amidst it all, the forgotten fragments of the *Epic of Gilgamesh* served as a haunting reminder of how stories, much like water, never truly disappear—they just take new forms.

And the ending? Simply breathtaking. It was one of those rare conclusions that make you sit in silence, absorbing its beauty. This book was not just a story—it was an experience. A slow, immersive, and deeply thought-provoking read that lingers long after the last page.

Would I recommend it? Absolutely. It’s not just a book—it’s a journey. 🌊✨

We picked *The Housemaid* as our April read for the **Chapter Chatters** book club, and I couldn’t be happier with the choice. This psychological thriller was fast-paced, full of suspense, and had me hooked right from the beginning. I ended up finishing it in just two days because I *needed* to know what would happen next!

The story revolves around Millie, a woman desperate for a fresh start who accepts a job as a live-in housemaid for the wealthy Winchester family. But as she settles into their luxurious home, it becomes clear that something isn’t right. Nina Winchester is unpredictable, the house is full of secrets, and Millie finds herself walking on eggshells. As the mystery unravels, you realize nothing is as it seems.

What really stood out to me was the way Freida McFadden builds tension. Each chapter ends on a mini cliffhanger, pushing you to keep turning the pages. And Millie’s transformation? Completely unexpected but brilliantly written. Just when you think you’ve figured her out, the story flips. That ending caught me totally off guard, but in the best way.

It’s the kind of thriller that plays with your mind and makes you question every character’s motive. I truly enjoyed reading it and am already tempted to dive into the second book in the series.

If you're into domestic thrillers, shocking plot twists, and fast reads that keep you on edge, *The Housemaid* is definitely worth picking up.

Personal notes:
Evie Woods is one of my auto-buy authors, and with *A Mysterious Bakery on Rue de Paris*, she once again delivers a beautiful blend of mystery, magic, love, and warmth. I had been eagerly waiting for this release, and it certainly didn’t disappoint. As always, Woods’ writing creates a cozy, heartwarming atmosphere that leaves me smiling long after I’ve turned the last page.


This book is about **Edie Lane**, who leaves behind her life in Ireland, chasing a dream job at a bakery in Paris. However, when she arrives, she finds herself not in Paris but in Compiègne, a charming little town with a bakery that has a reputation for magical pastries. The bakery’s treats are said to offer more than just deliciousness—they have the power to heal sorrow, unlock memories, and even reveal hidden desires. But Edie’s journey is more than just about finding a bakery; it’s about discovering herself, building new friendships, and finding a fresh start after loss.


What I absolutely loved about this book was how it captured the power of new beginnings and the healing process that comes with it. The bakery is more than a setting—it’s a symbol of second chances, fresh starts, and the unexpected magic that can come from embracing new opportunities. The characters were wonderfully real, each dealing with their own struggles, yet finding comfort and growth in the most unexpected ways. The mix of mystery surrounding the bakery’s magic, the light romance, and the underlying themes of love, loss, and renewal made this an unforgettable read.


As always, the happy endings that Woods crafts fill my heart with warmth. The story is a reminder that even when life takes us in unexpected directions, it often leads us exactly where we need to be. It’s a feel-good, uplifting read that will leave you believing in magic, love, and the beauty of starting over.

Title: Water Moon

Personal notes:
*Water Moon* had been on my TBR for the longest time, drawn in by its magical title and captivating cover. I wasn’t sure what to expect when I started reading, but I’m so glad I picked it up. It turned out to be a beautifully written and heartwarming fantasy that I absolutely loved.

The story follows **Hana Ishikawa**, who inherits a pawnshop in Tokyo where people can trade their deepest regrets. After her father goes missing and the shop is ransacked, Hana embarks on a magical journey with a young physicist to recover a stolen regret and uncover hidden truths. Along the way, they experience mystical worlds filled with rain puddles, paper cranes, and night markets in the clouds, all while Hana confronts a secret of her own.

What really stood out to me in this book was the lyrical, almost dreamlike writing. The blend of fantasy and reality felt seamless, creating a world that was magical yet emotionally grounded. The concept of pawning regrets was unique and thought-provoking, making me reflect on the choices we make and how they shape us. Hana's journey of self-discovery, healing, and confronting past choices was deeply moving.

The relationship between Hana and the physicist was tender and evolving, and the story’s pacing, while slow, allowed the emotional depth to unfold naturally. The magical elements, like the paper cranes and the mystical night market, added a sense of wonder without overshadowing the emotional core of the story.

*Water Moon* is a book that stays with you long after you’ve finished it. It’s whimsical, poignant, and filled with heart, making it a perfect read for anyone who enjoys magical realism and stories about healing, self-discovery, and letting go of regrets.

Personal notes:
We picked *Kaikeyi* as our monthly read for **Fates & Fabes**, our mythology book club—and I honestly couldn’t have asked for a better pick. This book completely changed the way I saw Kaikeyi, a character often painted as a villain in the age-old Ramayana.

Vaishnavi Patel’s narration is not only beautiful, but deeply thought-provoking. She gives Kaikeyi a voice—a story that’s raw, powerful, and incredibly human. For so long, we’ve heard the same tale where Kaikeyi is the reason for Ram’s exile. But this retelling invites readers to look beyond that one moment and truly understand the woman behind the myth.

Kaikeyi is strong, fierce, and unapologetically ambitious. She dares to question tradition, seeks justice for women, and tries to shape her own destiny in a world that constantly tries to silence her. I loved how the book made me pause and reflect on the image I’d grown up with. It made me rethink age-old beliefs, and that’s exactly the kind of storytelling I love—narratives that challenge, inspire, and empower.

This book has earned a permanent spot on my recommendation list. It’s one of the best books I’ve ever read—beautifully written, emotionally rich, and so relevant even today. If you love mythology retellings with strong female leads and layered storytelling, *Kaikeyi* is a must-read.

The Book That Wouldn’t Burn* by Mark Lawrence had been sitting on my shelf ever since I picked it up at the Delhi Book Fair—and it was the stunning cover and title that drew me in first. After all, who can resist a book about books? This is the first installment in the *Library Trilogy*, and as a book lover, I knew I had to dive in.

Set in a vast, ancient library filled with endless secrets, the story unfolds through two main characters—**Livira**, a fierce and curious girl taken from a life of survival in the Dust, and **Evar**, a quiet boy raised among books but shielded from the outside world. As their paths slowly converge across timelines and dimensions, the book takes you on a journey filled with mystery, philosophical questions, and the raw power of knowledge.

What I absolutely loved was the atmosphere—it’s dark, immersive, and full of wonder. The library itself almost becomes a living, breathing character with its endless stacks, hidden doors, and forbidden texts. The book is thrilling and mysterious, with so many layers of intrigue that kept me glued to the pages.

However, as the story progressed, the narrative began twisting through multiple timelines, time portals, and philosophical ideas that made it a bit too complex toward the end. At times, it felt like I was struggling to keep up with all the moving parts. But even with its confusion, Livira’s adventure kept me hooked. Her fiery spirit and curiosity were enough to push me through the dense parts of the story.

This is definitely a series that demands your full attention. I’m curious to see how things unfold in the next part—and with the third book on the horizon, I’ll be picking up Book 2 soon.

Title: Under the Whispering Door

Personal notes:
We picked this book for our May book club under the fantasy theme, and honestly? It started off a bit slow—we weren’t sure where it was headed. But by the end, *Under the Whispering Door* turned into such a heartwarming and unexpectedly profound read, it stayed with all of us.

The story begins at Wallace’s own funeral. Yes, you read that right. A reaper shows up to collect his soul, and soon Wallace finds himself at Charon’s Crossing—a quiet little tea shop run by Hugo, the kind ferryman who helps souls cross over. Wallace is not ready to move on though. He spent his life chasing success, forgetting how to actually live. But now, with only seven days to cross over, he sets out to experience a lifetime in that one week.

It’s hilarious in moments, haunting in others, but above all, incredibly kind. The book gently nudges you to think about grief, healing, purpose, and how we treat others—and ourselves. T.J. Klune has a unique way of blending fantasy with very real, very human emotions. And Hugo? He may just be the softest, most comforting character you’ll ever meet.

If you're in the mood for something cozy but reflective—with a cup of tea, perhaps—this one's for you. It might take a few chapters, but the emotional payoff is so worth it.

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ (4/5)
Quiet, quirky, and soul-soothing. Like a hug in book form.

The novel begins with an eight-year-old girl who dares to dream of marrying Prince Salim—and follows her extraordinary journey through heartbreak, court politics, and the maze of power. Through Indu Sundaresan’s evocative storytelling, we witness the emotional and political evolution of a woman who stood tall in a world built by men.

As someone who adores historical fiction, this book had me hooked from page one. The writing is rich, immersive, and full of texture. You can almost hear the whispers in Akbar’s court and feel the tension of power games behind the zenana walls. It’s a story of longing, strategy, and the courage it takes to change your fate.

If you’re drawn to strong female characters, royal settings, and intricately layered storytelling, this is a must-read. Indu Sundaresan does absolute justice to Mehrunnisa’s legacy—bold, intelligent, and unforgettable.

Set against the backdrop of wartime England, *The Booklover’s Library* is a deeply moving story of resilience, love, and the power of books to heal and connect us. Emma Taylor, a widow in Nottingham, faces an uphill battle to support her daughter Olivia amid legal restrictions that make it nearly impossible for widows with children to find work. When she finally lands a job at Boots’ Booklover’s Library, it’s more than just a paycheck—it becomes a lifeline.

As the threat of war becomes reality and Olivia is evacuated to the countryside, Emma is left alone, grappling with fear and uncertainty. But through the friendships she forms with her neighbors and coworkers, and through the books she recommends to the library’s quirky regulars, Emma begins to find solace and strength. The library is more than a workplace—it’s a place where stories come alive, memories of her late father and the bookstore they once shared return, and a community forms around a shared love for literature.

Adeline Martin’s storytelling shines in the way she captures both the harsh realities of wartime and the quiet moments of hope that keep people going. The mysterious disappearance of books adds a layer of intrigue that kept me turning the pages, but it’s the warmth of the relationships and the celebration of books as refuge that truly made this novel special.

The ending touched my heart deeply, reminding me of the magic in happy endings—not just in books, but in life. This story is a beautiful tribute to the strength of a mother’s love, the bonds we build in community, and the timeless comfort we find in stories. If you love historical fiction that stirs your soul and makes you believe in hope, this book is definitely one to read.

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ (5/5)
A heartfelt, uplifting read that celebrates the resilience of the human spirit and the transformative power of books.

Set in the hauntingly beautiful yet dangerous Sundarbans, this novel is as much about its characters as it is about the tides, the rivers, the dolphins, and the wild unpredictability of nature itself. Honestly, at times it felt like the real protagonist was the Sundarbans — fierce, mysterious, and deeply alive.

The first half of the book felt a little too detailed for me, with heavy descriptions that slowed the pace. But once I got past that, I found myself fully immersed — especially in the delicate, quiet bond between Piya and Fokir. Their moments were the most touching, filled with unspoken understanding and a rawness that made their connection unforgettable.

And Fokir... oh Fokir. 🌊
A man of few words, yet his presence lingered long after I turned the last page. His simplicity, courage, and gentle spirit stole my heart, making him my favourite character in the story.

Reading this book also left me in awe — and fear — of how people survive in the Sundarbans, surrounded by threats like tigers, crocodiles, snakes, and the ever-unpredictable tides. It’s a life unimaginable to many of us, and Ghosh captures it with chilling honesty.

As for the ending — I wasn’t sure what I expected, but it broke me. 💔 I kept wishing it had been different, hoping against hope that maybe, just maybe, my favourite character would be spared. But like the tide, this story doesn’t bend to our will.

A haunting, lyrical, and emotionally stirring read — worth the slow burn.

The plot unravels a secret passed from Ravan to Lakshman, said to hold the key to Ayodhya's future and the fate of humanity. Fast forward to the present, where industrialist Aditya Pillai and South Korean technocrat Somi Kim are caught in a deadly mission that ties past legends with present-day global tensions.

As always, Sanghi’s mastery lies in connecting ancient history with modern science, and turning it into a gripping political thriller. The scattered references to Kailasa, Pandya rule, and even South Korean myth made the story incredibly rich and layered.

Personal notes:
Every epic we know is shaped by voices we rarely hear. Koral Dasgupta’s Kunti, the third book in her Sati Series, gives that voice to one of the most pivotal yet misunderstood women of the Mahabharata.

Kunti is often remembered only as the mother of the Pandavas. But this retelling shows us a woman caught between destiny, duty, and desire. From the moment she invokes a boon that changes the course of her life, to her choices as a queen, a mother, and finally as a silent witness to the great war, her story is layered with power, vulnerability, and quiet strength.

Her series as a whole made me deeply curious about Indra—especially after reading Ahalya and now Kunti. It’s refreshing to experience these retellings of women whose tales are so often misinterpreted or overshadowed. Koral Dasgupta doesn’t just reimagine them; she reclaims their voices.

What strikes me most is her writing—it’s so lyrical that you feel the urge to highlight every line, to pause, to reread, and to share it with the world. There’s a tenderness in her words, even when she’s writing about pain or silence. She doesn’t glorify Kunti, nor does she diminish her. Instead, she paints her with all her flaws, emotions, and dilemmas, reminding us that even in epics, women are not just symbols—they are people.

Reading Kunti made me reflect on how stories often leave women in the background, while their choices ripple across generations. Through this retelling, you see the Mahabharata not as a distant legend, but as a deeply human story of love, duty, and consequence.

If you enjoyed Draupadi by Chitra Banerjee Divakaruni or Tara from the same series, Kunti will move you with its depth and sensitivity.

Sometimes the stories we know hide the voices we never hear. The Witch’s Heart does exactly that—it takes Norse mythology and retells it through the eyes of Angrboda, a witch often forgotten in the sagas, yet one whose choices shape the fate of gods.

Banished by Odin for refusing to share her knowledge of the future, Angrboda finds herself broken, wandering through the woods, and trying to rebuild a quiet life. But destiny finds her again when Loki enters her world. What begins as an unlikely companionship slowly grows into a bond filled with tenderness, wit, and heartbreak. From their love come children whose existence carries both doom and power—children the world fears, but a mother loves fiercely.

What I loved most about this book was how human it felt, despite being steeped in myth. Angrboda isn’t just a witch or a figure of prophecy—she is a woman who knows loss, love, sacrifice, and resilience. Her struggles and her strength make the story both intimate and epic. The pacing is gentle in the beginning, almost lulling you into her solitude, but soon pulls you into the whirl of fate, gods, and inevitable tragedy.

Genevieve Gornichec’s writing is lyrical without being heavy. It carries the ache of unspoken grief, the fire of defiance, and the quiet beauty of a mother’s love. This is not Loki’s story, nor Odin’s, nor even Ragnarok’s—it’s hers. A reminder that sometimes the most powerful stories are not of heroes and wars, but of the women who endure, love, and fight in the shadows.

If you enjoy mythology retellings like Circe or A Thousand Ships, this one will move you deeply. It’s a tale of love, loss, and courage—woven with magic and myth, yet painfully, beautifully human.

Through Nora’s journey of stepping into these alternate lives, Haig beautifully explores the “what ifs” we often carry in our hearts. The regrets, the dreams abandoned, the paths never taken—all come alive in a way that makes you pause and reflect on your own choices.

Personal notes:
There’s something irresistible about a gothic mystery—the kind that creeps into your imagination and refuses to leave. Wilkie Collins’ The Woman in White, first published in 1859, is one such story. Considered one of the earliest mystery novels, it continues to captivate readers with its eerie atmosphere, unforgettable characters, and intricate plot.

The novel begins with Walter Hartright’s late-night encounter with a mysterious woman dressed in white. From that moment, the tale spins into a web of secrets, lies, and sinister plots, centering around Laura Fairlie, her half-sister Marian Halcombe, and the unsettling Count Fosco. Told through multiple voices and shifting perspectives, the narrative becomes almost like a courtroom testimony—layered, fragmented, and yet irresistibly gripping.

What makes this novel so powerful is not just the mystery, but its psychological depth. Marian Halcombe, in particular, stands out as one of the strongest female characters in Victorian literature—fierce, intelligent, and unafraid to confront danger head-on. The interplay between light and dark, innocence and corruption, makes every chapter feel steeped in tension.

Reading The Woman in White is like stepping into a shadowy corridor where every turn could reveal betrayal or redemption. Collins blends gothic elements with early detective fiction so seamlessly that it feels timeless—even modern readers can sense echoes of his influence in today’s thrillers.

⭐ Rating: 4/5
A haunting, suspenseful masterpiece that set the stage for detective and gothic fiction alike. If you enjoy atmospheric mysteries with layered characters, this classic deserves a place on your shelf

Book Review – The Secret of Secrets by Dan Brown

Following Robert Langdon to Prague, the novel throws him into a shadowy city filled with labyrinthine passages, graveyards, and looming castles. Katherine Solomon’s sudden disappearance sparks a high-stakes chase where Langdon must navigate not just the city but a web of suspense and danger that feels more rooted in science fiction than the historical conspiracy thrillers we’ve loved him for.

Yet despite the shift, Brown’s storytelling remains captivating. The pacing is relentless, keeping me awake until 4 AM, turning pages to uncover twists I didn’t see coming. While I missed the intricate code-breaking and symbolic puzzles that usually define a Langdon novel, the suspense, unexpected turns, and sheer thrill of the hunt were enough to hold me completely engaged.

And yes—would I recommend it? Totally! Even if it’s a slightly different flavor of Brown, the story is gripping, the stakes are high, and the ending is completely unexpected. Fans of Langdon and thrillers will still find themselves hooked.

⭐ Rating: 4/5

Part of the *Lakefront Billionaires* series, this story follows Ellie Sinclair, a hopeless romantic and songwriter, and Rafael Lopez, a workaholic single dad. On paper, they have nothing in common, yet fate—and a summer trip—throws them together in ways neither expected.


What makes this book so addictive is the chemistry. Rafael’s grumpy-but-protective dad vibe colliding with Ellie’s warmth and charm creates a tension that crackles off the page. Old feelings resurface, boundaries blur, and the story balances humor, romance, and emotional stakes perfectly. Watching them navigate their shared responsibilities, flirtations, and personal insecurities keeps you hooked from start to finish.


Beyond the romance, the book captures relatable emotions: the vulnerability of letting someone close again, the push-pull of attraction and reason, and the joy of small moments turning into something bigger. Lauren Layne writes with charm and heart, making both characters feel real and their connection believable.

Title: The Liberation of Sita

One-line recommendation: A beautifully written, feminist retelling of the Ramayana that will challenge everything you thought you knew.
Personal notes:
The Liberation of Sita* is a powerful retelling of the *Ramayana* through the eyes of its women. In this feminist reimagining, Volga brings forth voices that were long silenced — Ahalya, Surpanakha, Renuka, Urmila, and Sita herself — showing how each woman discovers her own path to freedom, strength, and identity.

Every once in a while, you come across a book that quietly challenges everything you thought you knew — *The Liberation of Sita* by Volga is one such gem. This women-centric retelling offers a refreshing and powerful take on the female characters of the *Ramayana*, giving them voices, choices, and the space to define their own identities.

Translated from Telugu to English, this book beautifully reimagines Sita’s journey — not as a tale of suffering or endurance, but of awakening, strength, and self-realization. Each encounter Sita has with other women from the epic — Ahalya, Surpanakha, Renuka, and Urmila — brings a new layer of understanding and transformation. Through these stories, Volga paints a world where women reclaim their narratives and walk their own paths to liberation.

What I absolutely loved is how this book manages to be deeply philosophical yet so simply written that you can binge-read it in a single day. It’s short, impactful, and filled with lines that make you pause and reflect.

It’s no wonder this book is so hyped — it truly deserves every bit of appreciation it gets. If, like me, you love reading retellings of Indian scriptures from a woman’s perspective, this is an *absolute must-read*.

Totally recommended! 🌿✨

Title: Katabasis

One-line recommendation: A dark, imaginative, and emotionally complex tale of power, emotion, and redemption.
Personal notes:
After reading Babel, R.F. Kuang easily became one of those authors whose books I’ll pick up without a second thought. And Katabasis just reinforced that. This book was nothing short of a roller coaster — a wild mix of dark academia, magic, and a twist of hell that keeps you hooked till the very end.
If I talk about the romance, it carries that classic enemies-to-lovers tension that we all secretly love. The chemistry between the leads is sharp, layered, and full of those slow-burn moments that make you want to keep turning pages. But what really sets Katabasis apart is how Kuang blends mythology, power, and emotion into a story that’s both haunting and beautiful.
The ending was unexpected — not in a disappointing way, but in the kind that makes you sit back and think for a while. I can’t really say what I was expecting, but the way it all came together felt… right. And yes, somewhere between the chaos, darkness, and redemption, I found myself genuinely liking Peter, the male lead. His complexity adds so much depth to the story.
Overall, Katabasis is an absolute treat if you’re into books that explore hell, magic, and the intricate world of academia. It’s intense, imaginative, and filled with that signature Kuang touch — morally grey characters, emotional depth, and writing that lingers.
Definitely a recommended read!

One-line recommendation: A heartwarming and thrilling tale of identity, belonging, and redemption set against the backdrop of WWII Lisbon.
Personal notes:
Set against the sunlit streets of Lisbon during the turbulence of World War II, *The Bookshop of Secrets* is one of those quietly enchanting reads that pulls you in from the very first page. Kerry Barrett blends mystery, history, and heartfelt emotion into a story that feels both comforting and thrilling.

The novel follows **Lara Hope**, who arrives in Lisbon searching for a family she has never known, desperate for a fresh beginning after her father’s death. What she finds instead is a tender sense of belonging in her landlady’s serene little bookshop — a haven tucked into one of Lisbon’s most picturesque corners. But peace never lasts long in a world at war.

The turning point comes when Lara witnesses a customer secretly swapping a book. That moment unravels everything she thought she knew about the bookshop. Suddenly, Lara is swept into a web of coded messages, hidden identities, political secrets, and quiet acts of defiance. And yet, the book never loses its warmth — friendships bloom, love finds its gentle way in, and even royalty makes an appearance.

Barrett writes Lisbon beautifully — the alleys, the light, the sea breeze, the sense of a city untouched yet deeply affected by war. It’s atmospheric without being heavy. The mystery is engaging without being overwhelming. Most of all, Lara’s journey feels deeply personal: a woman trying to build a new life while unintentionally stepping into a dangerous, exhilarating one.

What makes this novel special is how it balances heart and intrigue. It’s a book about finding courage, discovering unexpected connections, and learning that sometimes the life we’re meant for is nothing like the one we imagined.

A cosy, charming historical mystery with just enough shadows to keep you turning the pages. Perfect for readers who love bookshops, wartime secrets, and heroines who grow into their strength. ✨📚

Title: The Architect's Apprentice
Author: Elif Shafak

One-line recommendation: A richly detailed and atmospheric tale of passion, architecture, and devotion set in the heart of the Ottoman Empire.
Personal notes:
Elif Shafak has a way of transporting readers to worlds that feel both distant and alive, and *The Architect’s Apprentice* is one such unforgettable journey. Set in the vibrant heart of the Ottoman Empire, the story follows Jahan, a young elephant keeper who is swept into the dazzling yet dangerous world of the royal court. What begins as a boy’s bond with an elephant grows into a sweeping tale of ambition, loyalty, love, and destiny.

What I loved most is how Shafak paints Istanbul—its minarets, marketplaces, mosques, and mysteries—with such richness that you can almost hear the sounds and smell the spices. Through Jahan’s eyes, we witness the rise of Sinan, the legendary imperial architect, and the making of architectural marvels that still stand today. Their apprentice-master relationship feels deeply human: full of curiosity, wisdom, and quiet lessons about craft and character.

The book moves like a tapestry—threads of history, fiction, Sufi philosophy, and magical realism woven into each chapter. The characters feel flawed yet real, especially Jahan, whose innocence and longing shape his path. The elephant, Chota, becomes more than a companion; he becomes a symbol of purity in a world driven by politics and power.

It’s not a fast-paced story, but a meditative one—slow, atmospheric, beautifully detailed. Some parts may feel dense, but that’s also the charm of the book: it allows you to linger, observe, and soak in the era.

Overall, *The Architect’s Apprentice* is a lyrical, immersive read for anyone who loves historical fiction with soul. It reminds you that journeys shape us as much as destinations do—and that sometimes, the smallest beginnings lead to the grandest stories.

Perfect for readers who enjoy books that take them to another time, another city, another heartbeat entirely. ✨

Title: Mate (Bride, #2)
Author: Ali Hazelwood
Themes: fated mates; belonging; identity; political intrigue; survival; destiny vs free will

One-line recommendation: An explosive, high-stakes paranormal romance packed with intense chemistry, dangerous political intrigue, and unforgettable characters.
Personal notes:
Ali Hazelwood returns to her supernatural universe with *Mate*, a gripping, emotional, high-stakes companion novel to *Bride* — this time following **Serena Paris**, the first-ever Human-Were hybrid, and **Koen Alexander**, the fiercely powerful Alpha who would burn down the world to protect her.

From the very beginning, Serena’s story pulls you in. Orphaned, hunted, and carrying the weight of an entire species’ hopes on her shoulders, she has never truly belonged anywhere. Coming forward as a hybrid was supposed to unite Humans, Vampyres, and Weres — but instead, it turned her into a political lightning rod. Everyone wants to use her. Everyone wants to control her. And someone definitely wants her dead.

Enter Koen.
The Alpha of the Northwest pack. Commanding, lethal, loyal. A man whose instincts have already chosen Serena as his mate — even if she wants absolutely nothing to do with destiny, fate, or the bond tying them together. Their dynamic is explosive: the guarded, wary girl who’s never been safe, and the Alpha who would raze kingdoms before letting harm reach her.

Hazelwood balances tension, danger, and slow-burn emotion beautifully. This isn’t just a romance; it’s a survival story. Serena’s past catches up with her in ways she cannot outrun, and the political landscape is even more dangerous than in *Bride*. The Vampyres, the packs, the Humans — everyone has a stake, and Serena stands right at the centre of the storm.

What makes *Mate* so captivating is the emotional payoff. Serena’s inner strength, her fear of connection, Koen’s unwavering devotion, their push-and-pull — everything feels raw and real. The protective Alpha trope is strong, but Serena’s resilience ensures the relationship stays balanced.

If you loved *Bride*, *Mate* delivers even higher stakes, deeper emotion, and a heroine you can’t help rooting for.

A thrilling, romantic, fast-paced continuation of Hazelwood’s supernatural world — with all the found-family warmth, political danger, and crackling chemistry you expect. 🐺🔥💙

Title: The Women of Troy (Women of Troy, #2)
Author: Pat Barker
Themes: grief; captivity; survival; war aftermath; resilience; womanhood

One-line recommendation: An unflinching myth retelling that strips away romantic heroism to highlight the raw human cost of war borne by women.
Personal notes:
Pat Barker returns to the aftermath of the Trojan War with a powerful, unflinching narrative that gives voice to those history often silences — the women. *The Women of Troy* picks up after the fall of Troy, but instead of focusing on heroes and victories, Barker draws us into the quiet, suffocating world of grief, captivity, and survival.

At the centre of the story is Briseis, now pregnant and living among the Greek victors who destroyed her city. Through her eyes, we witness the unsettling calm after the chaos — a camp full of restless soldiers waiting for the winds to change so they can sail home, while the Trojan women struggle to hold on to their dignity, identity, and hope. The contrast is haunting: the Greeks who won the war feel lost, while the women they conquered somehow stand stronger in spirit.

What makes this book special is Barker’s writing — sharp, human, painfully honest. She doesn’t romanticize myth; she strips it down to its raw emotions. The anger of the Trojan women, the guilt simmering among the soldiers, the suffocating tension inside the camp, and the eerie presence of the dead — everything feels intensely real.

Briseis continues to be one of the most compelling narrators in myth retellings. Her resilience is quiet but powerful. Even surrounded by men who see her as spoils of war, she finds ways to resist, support others, and hold on to her sense of self. Barker also beautifully highlights the bonds between women — fragile, tender, and necessary for survival.

*The Women of Troy* isn’t a fast-paced myth retelling. It’s a slow burn, as heavy and atmospheric as the still air the Greeks wait through. But it’s also deeply moving — a reminder that even after wars end, the battles of women begin.

Perfect for readers who love feminist retellings, Greek mythology told with grit, and stories that echo long after you close the book. ✨

Title: The Chola Tigers: Avengers of Somnath
Author: Amish Tripathi
Themes: vengeance; unity across regions; grief and loss; dharma and duty; heroism from ordinary lives; nation's pain transformed into purpose

One-line recommendation: A gripping, emotionally charged historical thriller that turns India’s darkest hour into an epic tale of vengeance and unity.
Personal notes:
Amish Tripathi’s *The Chola Tigers* is a fierce, emotionally charged historical thriller that begins in the aftermath of one of the darkest chapters of Indian history — the brutal raid of Somnath in 1025 CE. With the Shiva Linga destroyed and thousands dead, the pain of Bharat hangs heavy. But from that ruin rises a promise… and a vengeance that will shake empires.

The novel follows **five extraordinary individuals**, each from a different corner of India —
a fearless Tamil warrior,
a sharp-witted Gujarati merchant,
a devoted pilgrim of Lord Ayyappa,
a scholar-emperor from Malwa,
and the mighty Rajendra Chola himself, ruler of the world’s most powerful naval empire.

Bound by grief, rage, and Dharma, these five come together to undertake an impossible mission: to carry the war back to Ghazni and strike Mahmud where he believes he is untouchable.

What makes this book so addictive is how Amish blends **historical detail with blockbuster storytelling**. The scale is massive — the Chola naval fleet, the grandeur of Thanjavur, the political intensity of Malwa, and the chilling brutality of Ghazni’s court. Every chapter feels cinematic, full of momentum, filled with strategy, travel, espionage, and fire-forged camaraderie.

But beneath the adventure lies something deeply emotional:
✨ A story of unity beyond caste, region, or faith
✨ A nation’s pain transforming into purpose
✨ Heroes rising from ordinary lives
✨ The idea that vengeance, when tied to justice, becomes Dharma

Amish excels at creating characters who feel real — flawed, determined, and shaped by their personal losses. Rajendra Chola stands out as a powerful yet humane ruler, while the other four heroes bring heart, humour, and intensity to the mission.

*The Chola Tigers* is not just a tale of revenge; it’s a tale of resilience. Of a wounded civilization choosing courage over despair. Of five unlikely heroes carrying the honour of an entire nation on their shoulders.

Thrilling, patriotic, and emotionally stirring — this is Amish at his finest. A roaring tribute to unity, bravery, and Bharat. 🐅🔥🇮🇳

Title: Sons of Darkness (The Raag of Rta, #1)
Author: Gourav Mohanty
Publisher: Head of Zeus -- an AdAstra Book

One-line recommendation: A thrilling, cinematic epic fantasy perfect for fans of Game of Thrones looking for a dark, complex Indian mythology retelling.
Personal notes:
If Mahabharata met *Game of Thrones*, the result would look a lot like *Son of Darkness*. Gaurav Mohanty builds an epic world that is dark, political, magical, and unapologetically grand — the kind of fantasy that pulls you into its war-scarred kingdoms and refuses to let you leave.

The story reimagines ancient India through a brutal, fast-paced lens where gods, warriors, assassins, mystics, and monsters collide. Mohanty takes inspiration from Indian mythology but layers it with grit, ambition, and a modern, cinematic flair. The result is a mythology-inspired fantasy that feels familiar yet entirely new.

At the heart of the book is **Krishna**, not the flute-playing deity we grew up with — but a cunning, strategic, morally complex force whose presence shapes everyone around him. The characters are sharp, layered, and often operating in the gray spaces between duty and desire. You can’t predict who will remain loyal, who will betray, or who will survive… and that’s what makes it addictive.

The world-building is massive — kingdoms on the brink of war, secret societies, dark prophecies, deadly creatures, political intrigue, and ancient powers awakening from the shadows. Every chapter feels like a puzzle piece snapping into place, expanding the scale of the story. And the action? Brutal, visual, and thrilling.

What I personally loved is how Mohanty blends mythology with high fantasy without losing emotional depth. Despite the chaos, the book never forgets its characters — their fears, trauma, ambition, and silent battles. The dialogues are sharp, the twists are wild, and the moral dilemmas hit hard.

*Son of Darkness* is not a light read — it’s dense, bold, and packed with details — but that’s exactly why it’s so rewarding. If you enjoy complex epics, morally grey heroes, mythology retellings with a dark edge, and sprawling political drama, this book is a must-read.

A fierce, gripping, larger-than-life fantasy that keeps you hooked till the last page. ⚔️🔥✨

Title: The Secret History
Author: Donna Tartt
Themes: obsession; guilt; morality; class and privilege; isolation; intellectual hubris

Seasonal: Autumn; Back to School; rainy day read; Halloween
Collections: World Bookshelf; Civilizations Through Books; Civilization · Greece; Around the World in 52 Books; Heartbreaking Reads; Dark & Atmospheric; Page-Turners
One-line recommendation: The foundational dark academia novel that brilliantly dissects obsession, privilege, and the haunting weight of guilt.
Personal notes:
If a group of elite students, an isolated college town, Greek classics, and a murder told right at the beginning sounds intriguing — *The Secret History* pulls you in with exactly that promise.

Donna Tartt doesn’t rush this story. She lets it simmer. Slowly. Almost stubbornly. The book follows a tight-knit group of classics students whose intellectual world feels detached from reality, guided by the enigmatic Professor Julian. From the outside, everything looks refined and beautiful — knowledge, privilege, aesthetics — but underneath, something deeply unsettling brews.

I’ll be honest: this was a **long read**, and for me, the real hook arrived only after the halfway mark. The suspense is there from the start, but the emotional grip took its own sweet time. Once it did, I understood why people talk about this book the way they do — the tension, the moral decay, the quiet dread — all very intentional.

I can’t say I had a favorite character. If anything, that ambiguity feels deliberate. I was certain, however, that I didn’t like Bunny — nor his family — and I’m still unsure what to make of Professor Julian. Was he a mentor, a manipulator, or simply an observer who chose silence over responsibility? The book never hands you clear answers, and that discomfort stays with you.

The **dark academia vibe** is undeniable — libraries, rituals, intellectual arrogance, and beauty laced with darkness. That said, after reading *Babel*, I went into this with different expectations. *The Secret History* is quieter, slower, and less confrontational in comparison.

Would I reread it? Probably not.
Do I get the hype? Yes, I do.

This isn’t a book meant to be loved easily — it’s meant to be **felt**, questioned, and sat with long after the final page.

Title: Daughter of the Moon Goddess (The Celestial Kingdom, #1)
Author: Sue Lynn Tan
Themes: filial piety; sacrifice; resilience; identity; duty vs love
Tropes: hidden royalty; court intrigue; love triangle; training arc
Tags: Chinese mythology; dragons; AAPI author; book club pick; fantasy romance; debut novel; level:advanced
