One-line recommendation: A luminous, mythic fantasy steeped in Chinese folklore, featuring revered dragons, quiet resilience, and breathtaking world-building.
Personal notes:
Some stories feel like moonlight — quiet, luminous, and powerful in ways you don’t immediately realize. *The Daughter of the Moon Goddess* is one of those stories.

Inspired by Chinese mythology, Sue Lynn Tan introduces us to Xingyin, the hidden daughter of the Moon Goddess, who has grown up in secrecy, unaware of the dangerous truth surrounding her existence. When her world is suddenly thrown into chaos, she is forced to leave the moon and step into the Celestial Kingdom — a place filled with magic, political intrigue, trials of strength, and destinies far greater than she ever imagined.

I loved this book. Truly.
It has everything I look for in fantasy — **rich world-building, emotional depth, quiet resilience, and magic that feels ancient and reverent rather than loud**. And then there are the dragons — wise, revered, majestic beings who command respect rather than fear. After *Fourth Wing*, I didn’t think my love for dragons could grow any deeper, but this book proved me wrong in the most beautiful way.

What stood out to me most was Xingyin’s journey. She isn’t loud or reckless; her strength lies in patience, loyalty, and perseverance. Her growth feels earned, shaped by loss, love, and difficult choices. The emotional arcs — especially around sacrifice and longing — are tender and haunting, lingering long after you turn the last page.

The writing itself feels lyrical, almost poetic, making the reading experience immersive and slow in the best way possible. This is the kind of fantasy that invites you to pause, imagine, and sink into its world rather than rush through it.

If you love mythology-inspired fantasy, celestial realms, powerful yet gentle heroines, and dragons that feel like legends come alive — this book deserves a place on your shelf.

A story woven with magic, moonlight, and quiet courage — one I already know will stay with me for a long time 🌙✨

Title: Heart of the Sun Warrior (The Celestial Kingdom, #2)
Author: Sue Lynn Tan
Themes: sacrifice; duty vs love; loyalty; grief; identity; family
Tropes: love triangle; gods and mortals; royalty; quest
Tags: Chinese mythology; Asian author; celestial fantasy; duology finale; book club pick; AAPI author; level:intermediate
Seasonal: AAPI Heritage Month; Autumn read; rainy day read
Collections: World Bookshelf; Civilizations Through Books; Civilization · China; Around the World in 52 Books; East Asia Shelf; Heartbreaking Reads; Dark & Atmospheric
One-line recommendation: An emotionally charged, lushly written celestial fantasy that brings Xingyin's story to a powerful and breathtaking close.
Personal notes:
Sequels often carry the weight of expectations, and *The Heart of the Sun Warrior* rises to that challenge with emotional depth and quiet intensity.

Picking up after *The Daughter of the Moon Goddess*, this story finds Xingyin no longer the sheltered girl we first met, but a woman shaped by loss, duty, and the consequences of her own choices. The world expands beyond familiar celestial spaces into darker, more uncertain territories, where alliances are fragile and every decision comes at a cost.

What stood out to me most in this book was how **emotionally heavy** it felt. The conflicts are no longer just external — they live within Xingyin herself. Her growth is painful, slow, and deeply human. She learns that love, power, and loyalty rarely exist without sacrifice, and that real strength often lies in endurance rather than victory.

One aspect I didn’t expect was how my feelings toward the **Cloud Realm prince** evolved. What began as indifference slowly turned into understanding, and eventually, a quiet fondness. His arc is layered with restraint, responsibility, and unspoken emotion — the kind that doesn’t demand attention but earns it over time. That gradual shift made the emotional tension of the story even more compelling.

The magic remains lush and immersive, and the dragons continue to feel wise, revered, and awe-inspiring — creatures of legend rather than spectacle. There is a noticeable shift in tone compared to the first book; this one is darker, more complex, and at times, heartbreaking.

The pacing does slow down in parts, leaning more toward emotional buildup than action. But for me, that slowness allowed the weight of each choice and consequence to truly settle.

*The Heart of the Sun Warrior* is a thoughtful, emotional conclusion — one that doesn’t offer easy resolutions, but instead leaves you reflecting on growth, sacrifice, and the quiet cost of love long after the final page 🌙✨

Title: Days at the Torunka Café (Days at the Torunka Café, #1)
Author: Satoshi Yagisawa
Themes: healing; loneliness; human connection; everyday life; comfort; reflection
Tags: Japanese author; translated fiction; cozy read; under 300 pages; coffee shop setting; slow living; book club pick
Seasonal: rainy day read; autumn read; winter cozy read; weekend read
Collections: World Bookshelf; Civilizations Through Books; Civilization · Japan; Around the World in 52 Books; East Asia Shelf; Comfort Reads
One-line recommendation: A warm, soul-soothing slice-of-life read perfect for anyone seeking quiet comfort and soft human connection over a hot drink.
Personal notes:
Some books don’t demand your attention — they gently ask for it. *Days at the Torunka Café* is one such quiet, comforting read that feels like a warm cup of coffee on a slow afternoon.

Set in a small, unassuming café, this story follows the lives of people who drift in and out of Torunka — each carrying their own worries, loneliness, and unspoken thoughts. The café becomes more than just a place to eat or drink; it turns into a pause button in their lives, a space where time slows down and emotions are allowed to surface gently.

This is not a plot-heavy book. Nothing dramatic happens, and that’s exactly the charm. The beauty of this story lies in its simplicity — in everyday conversations, shared meals, and fleeting connections between strangers who may never meet again, yet leave a lasting imprint.

What I appreciated most was how the book captures the quiet weight of ordinary lives. The characters feel real — flawed, tired, hopeful in small ways. There’s a soft sense of healing woven through the narrative, not in a loud or life-altering manner, but in subtle shifts of perspective. It reminds you that sometimes comfort comes not from solutions, but from being seen and heard, even briefly.

The writing is calm and soothing, making this an ideal slow read. I found myself lingering over pages, not because I was desperate to know what happens next, but because I didn’t want to rush the experience. This is the kind of book you read alongside chai or coffee, in between moments of your own day.

If you enjoy slice-of-life stories, Japanese-style cozy fiction, and books that feel like a gentle exhale, *Days at the Torunka Café* is worth picking up.

A quiet story about ordinary days, shared spaces, and the small comfort of simply existing — sometimes, that’s all we need 🤍☕📚

Title: Dance of Shadows (The Raag of Rta, #2)
Author: Gourav Mohanty
Publisher: Head of Zeus -- an AdAstra Book
Themes: ancient secrets; power and politics; duty and destiny; ambition; mythological heritage
Tropes: quest for a lost city; dragons; ancient prophecy; slow burn romance
Tags: Indian author; epic fantasy; Indian mythology inspired; dragons; thick book; high stakes quest; sequel; level:advanced
Collections: India Bookshelf; Roots of Bharat; Indian Mythology Retellings; Dark & Atmospheric
One-line recommendation: An exhilarating, dragon-infused dark epic fantasy that masterfully blends Indian mythology with high-stakes, treasure-hunt intrigue.
Personal notes:
Sequels can either deepen a story or simply extend it — Dance of Shadows firmly does the former.

The second book in Gaurav Mohanty’s epic fantasy series, following The Son of Darkness, builds a world that feels richer, darker, and far more immersive. I’ll be honest: I enjoyed this part more than the first. The narrative has layers — of magic, politics, ancient history, and emotions — all unfolding at a more confident pace.

What truly stood out to me was the sense of adventure. The exploration of the lost city of Manu, especially through Nala and Parshuram’s journey, gave me strong vibes of a high-stakes treasure hunt. Reading those sections felt like stepping into a story where ancient secrets are waiting to be unearthed — the kind of tension and curiosity I associate with Dan Brown or Matthew Reilly novels. That blend of mythology and fast-moving discovery kept me completely hooked.

The book balances its elements beautifully. There’s magic woven into the worldbuilding, not overwhelming but deeply rooted. The romance simmers quietly in the background, adding emotional depth without overpowering the larger narrative. And then there are the dragons — majestic, powerful, and absolutely my favorite part. Their presence elevates the story, adding both awe and intensity whenever they appear.

What I appreciated most was how the story doesn’t rely on spectacle alone. The characters feel more grounded, their motivations clearer, and the stakes more personal. The writing feels sharper, and the plot more assured, as if the author truly settles into his world in this installment.

Dance of Shadows is the kind of sequel that expands its universe while keeping the reader emotionally invested. If you enjoy mythology-inspired fantasy with ancient cities, layered storytelling, and dragons that command attention, this book is a rewarding read.

A powerful continuation — one that proves the series is only getting stronger 🐉✨📖

Title: Immortal
Author: Sue Lynn Tan

One-line recommendation: A dreamlike, emotional fantasy romance perfect for fans of slow-burn enemies-to-lovers stories filled with yearning and rich worldbuilding.
Personal notes:
A mortal ruler bound to her land.
An immortal God of War sworn to destruction.
And a slow-burn, enemies-to-lovers romance that unfolds across time, duty, and longing.

*Immortal* by **Sue Lynn Tan**, the author of *The Daughter of the Moon Goddess*, tells the story of the Lady of Tianxia and the God of War — two powerful beings forced into reluctant proximity by fate and circumstance. What begins as mistrust and resistance slowly transforms into something tender, restrained, and deeply emotional.

This book leans heavily into **atmosphere and emotion** rather than fast-paced action. The romance is the heart of the story — unhurried, filled with tension, and shaped by sacrifice. Every interaction feels deliberate, making the eventual softening between the two characters feel earned rather than rushed. If you enjoy enemies-to-lovers where the shift is gradual and rooted in mutual respect, this will speak to you.

The writing is lyrical and calm, creating a dreamlike reading experience. The magic here isn’t explosive; it exists quietly in immortality, ancient vows, and the weight of time. Sue Lynn Tan excels at portraying longing — the kind that lingers between words, in pauses, in what remains unsaid.

Compared to the Celestial Kingdom duology, *Immortal* has a simpler plot, but emotionally, it carries just as much depth. Themes of duty versus desire, the cost of eternal life, and the fragility of mortal moments are woven beautifully throughout the narrative.

This isn’t a book meant to be devoured in one sitting. It’s meant to be read slowly, perhaps when you’re craving something soft yet intense, romantic yet restrained.

For readers who loved mythology-inspired fantasy, slow-burn romance, and the gentle magic of Sue Lynn Tan’s storytelling, *Immortal* is a quiet, aching kind of love story — one that stays with you long after the final page 🌙📖✨

Title: The Blind King
Author: S. Deepanshu

Tags: Indian author; Mahabharata retelling; mythological fiction; post-war story; book club pick; philosophical read; level:intermediate

One-line recommendation: A moving, introspective retelling that turns away from the battlefield to explore the human weight of guilt and redemption.
Personal notes:
What sets 'The Blind King' apart from the countless retellings of the Mahabharata is its stunning shift in focus. Instead of walking us through the familiar events of the epic, this book turns its gaze to what most authors leave untouched—the silence after the war, the ruins left behind, and the heavy, suffocating aftermath that no victory can erase.

This is not the story of the Kurukshetra war. This is the story of what comes 'after'.

Through an unforgettable conversation between Krishna and Dhritarashtra, the book explores emotions that are surprisingly universal. As Dhritarashtra confronts the choices he made, the blame he placed on others, and the regrets that refused to loosen their grip, you can’t help but see reflections of your own life. The “what-ifs,” the guilt, the fear of owning our mistakes—these are not just the king’s burdens; they’re ours too. And that’s where the book truly becomes more than mythology—it becomes deeply human.

The writing is fluid, and the conversations flow with a natural ease, effortlessly weaving past events into the present moment. I especially loved how the last few chapters bring everything together with such emotional clarity. There’s a quiet power in the way the story concludes, almost as if both Dhritarashtra and the reader arrive at the same point of acceptance.

'The Blind King' isn’t just another Mahabharata-inspired retelling. It’s a rare, introspective journey into responsibility, regret, healing, and the courage it takes to face your own truth. A unique and beautifully crafted book that lingers long after the final page.

Personal notes:
'A Language of Dragons' is one of those debuts that doesn’t just intrigue you — it seizes you from page one and refuses to let go. Set in an alternative 1923 London where dragons fly overhead and rebellion simmers beneath the city’s polished façade, this novel blends Dark Academia, political intrigue, and slow-burn romance into an unforgettable fantasy.

Vivien Featherswallow is the perfect Dark Academia heroine: brilliant, tightly wound, terrified of stepping out of line, and carrying the weight of her family’s survival on her shoulders. Her carefully planned life collapses in a single night — a spark that ignites civil war, leaving her parents imprisoned and her sister missing. What begins as an academic ambition turns into a desperate, high-stakes quest for freedom.

Her recruitment into Bletchley Park — a secretive hub of codebreaking infused with dragon lore — is where the story truly soars. The atmosphere is deliciously tense: whispered secrets, dangerous missions, hidden identities, and a mysterious dragon language that refuses to be decoded. As Viv delves deeper, she uncovers truths that shatter everything she thought she understood about her country, her privilege, and the war she’s unknowingly helped fuel.

The book is rich with Dark Academia vibes: coded messages, dusty libraries, moral complexity, and the intoxicating thrill of forbidden knowledge. Add to that a slow-burn enemies-to-lovers romance threaded through betrayal, loyalty, and razor-sharp chemistry, and it becomes utterly addictive.

With its sweeping world-building, political depth, and emotional intensity, 'A Language of Dragons' feels like a perfect blend of 'Babel', 'Fourth Wing'. It’s epic yet intimate, sharp yet tender — a debut that promises an extraordinary new voice in fantasy.

This isn’t just a story about dragons. It’s about power, privilege, rebellion, and the dangerous beauty of a language that could burn the world down… or save it.

Title: The Pearl That Broke Its Shell
Author: Nadia Hashimi
Genres: Historical Fiction; Literary Fiction; Cultural Fiction
Themes: identity; gender roles; resilience; survival; freedom; family dynamics; tradition
Tropes: dual timeline; disguise; secret identity; generational connection
Tags: Afghan author; women's rights; dual timeline fiction; book club pick; bacha posh; Middle Eastern setting; Women's History Month; level:intermediate
Seasonal: Women's History Month; Autumn read; book club pick
Collections: World Bookshelf; Middle East & North Africa; Around the World in 52 Books; Heartbreaking Reads; Comfort Reads; Dark & Atmospheric
One-line recommendation: A deeply moving and resilient dual-timeline story of two Afghan women fighting for freedom across generations.
Personal notes:
Nadia Hashimi is one of those authors I will pick up without even reading the blurb — because every book of hers does something rare: it breaks your heart, but it never abandons you in the darkness. Instead, she offers a fragile but steady thread of hope, the kind that reminds you that survival itself is a kind of victory.
*The Pearl That Broke the Shell* is the perfect example of this.

In this novel, Hashimi tells the parallel stories of two Afghan women separated by a hundred years, yet connected through the same fight for autonomy. Rahima, living in Kabul in 2009, grows up in a house where five daughters are not enough to earn respect, safety, or even basic freedom. Her world is painfully small — reduced further by her father’s addiction and the suffocating restrictions placed on girls. Everything changes the moment she becomes a *bacha posh*, temporarily allowed to live as a boy. This transformation opens a door she never imagined: access, mobility, education, and the intoxicating taste of choice.

A century earlier, in 1909, Shekiba’s story unfolds with equal weight. Disfigured as a child and treated as less than human, Shekiba’s life is a brutal portrait of how cruelty is often disguised as tradition. And yet, through unimaginable circumstances, she finds her way into the king’s palace, disguised as a man and serving as a guard. Even in her harshest moments, she discovers strength, resilience, and eventually, a future she never allowed herself to dream of.

What makes this novel unforgettable is how Hashimi weaves these two timelines into a conversation — about womanhood, survival, identity, and the quiet ways hope passes from one generation to the next. Rahima and Shekiba don’t just mirror each other; they amplify each other’s courage. Their stories illuminate the reality of countless Afghan women whose resilience is often invisible, unheard, or forgotten.

This book is painful, powerful, and deeply human. It lingers — not as a tragedy, but as a reminder of how fiercely women fight for the smallest sliver of freedom, and how that fight can echo across time.

Title: Beyond The Blinding Sun
Author: Jayanta G. Borpujari
Themes: exploitation; survival; hope; desperation; dignity; freedom
Tags: Indian author; translated fiction; book club pick; under 300 pages; social justice; immigration story; level:intermediate
Collections: India Bookshelf; Indian Literary Fiction; Heartbreaking Reads; Comfort Reads; Dark & Atmospheric; Page-Turners
One-line recommendation: A heart-wrenching and thought-provoking exploration of modern-day slavery and the struggles of immigrant laborers.
Personal notes:
This book doesn’t ask for your comfort — it takes it away.

'Beyond the Blinding Sun' is a brutal, unflinching portrayal of 'modern-day slavery', Set in Oman, told through the lives of three immigrants who leave home chasing dignity and survival, only to be swallowed by exploitation on foreign land. What they encounter isn’t just cruelty from individuals, but a system designed to trap, silence, and break them.

The 'first half' is emotionally traumatic. It sits heavy with fear, humiliation, hunger, and helplessness. The characters feel painfully real — vulnerable, exhausted, yet still trying to hold on to fragments of hope. Their suffering is quiet, repetitive, and degrading, which makes it even harder to read.

The 'second half' shifts into high tension and relentless suspense. As patience wears thin, desperation takes over. Escapes are planned, risks are taken, and survival becomes a gamble against detention centers, deserts, and ruthless authorities. The pace quickens, but the dread never fully lifts.

What makes this story deeply disturbing is how little it feels like fiction. This is the lived reality of countless unskilled and low-skilled immigrant labourers across the world — people promised work and opportunity, only to be trapped in contracts that strip them of freedom and dignity. Not everyone escapes. Not everyone is rescued. The book makes it painfully clear that survival often comes down to luck, rare intervention, or sheer endurance, while many others remain invisible inside the same cruel machinery.

The writing is fast-paced, accessible, and direct — but it leaves you sitting with uncomfortable questions long after you finish. This is not a feel-good read. It is an **important** one.

Title: The Lost Story

One-line recommendation: A quiet, emotional, and layered exploration of trauma, survival, and the power of friendship.
Personal notes:
The Lost Story* begins where most stories end — with two boys who vanished into a forest and somehow returned six months later. Fifteen years on, the mystery hasn’t faded; it has only changed shape. Trauma lingers, memories fracture, and the truth waits patiently to be confronted.

This is a story about **friendship, memory, guilt, and the cost of survival**. Jeremy remembers what truly happened. Rafe doesn’t. And that imbalance — of knowledge, protection, and secrecy — becomes the emotional core of the book. Add Emilie, desperately searching for her missing sister, and the past is forced open.

The magical realm here isn’t just beautiful or dangerous — it’s haunting. It feels like a place shaped by fear, wonder, and unfinished emotions. The fantasy elements are rich, but the real magic lies in how the story explores **what trauma erases, what love hides, and what truth demands**.

This book is quiet, emotional, and layered. It’s less about adventure and more about **reckoning** — about returning to the place that broke you in order to reclaim what was lost. Some parts feel heavy, some tender, and some deeply unsettling in the best way.

If you enjoy stories that blend fantasy with emotional depth, grief, and healing — this one will stay with you long after the last page.

Each chapter introduces a different customer, someone carrying their own loneliness, regret, or uncertainty. Through their encounters with Kogetsu and his magical confections, their lives shift — not magically solved, but gently realigned. What makes the book even more touching is that Kogetsu himself is on a journey too, slowly revealing his past and learning lessons alongside those he helps.

The writing is soft, comforting, and reflective. There’s no urgency here, no high-stakes conflict — just moments of human vulnerability, kindness, and quiet growth. It’s the kind of book you read slowly, preferably with tea nearby, letting each story linger.

If you enjoy **cozy fantasy, interconnected stories, and books that feel like a warm hug**, this one is a small, glowing delight 🍬✨

Let’s start with the cover—stunning, intriguing, and perfectly setting the mood for what’s inside. Having read the first part of the sequel, I was excited to see where the lives of Raaj, Ravi, and Bhanu would go. Three years later, we’re thrown straight into their world—a high-stakes ride where loyalties are tested, threats loom large, and friendships prove unshakeable.

At the heart of the story lies an unexpected twist: national security. This element elevates the book to an entirely new level. A special shout-out to the author for breaking down complex cybersecurity concepts so effortlessly that even readers with zero technical background can follow and enjoy every bit.

The suspense and thrill kept me on edge, yet Raaj’s witty banter made sure I never stopped smiling. If you’ve read the first part and enjoyed it, you're absolutely going to fall in love with this one.

And when you finally reach the end? The last page leaves you with a delightful surprise—one that’ll make you immediately ask the author, “When is the next part coming?”

Whether you're an adolescent, a young adult, or a tech-curious teen obsessed with hacking and cyber dynamics, this book has something for everyone. That’s the true beauty of it.

Title: GULNORA
Author: Ashok Bhasin
Themes: corruption; power games; identity; morality
Tags: Indian author; thriller; crime fiction; book club pick; translated fiction
Collections: India Bookshelf; Dark & Atmospheric; Page-Turners
One-line recommendation: A gripping thriller that will keep you on the edge of your seat until the very end.
Personal notes:
Some books don’t ask for your time politely—they demand it. GulNora is exactly that kind of book. A fast-paced, edge-of-the-seat thriller that kept me hooked late into the night, willingly sacrificing sleep just to read “one more chapter.”

The story begins in 2000 with a seemingly routine smuggling case at Delhi airport, where a young Uzbek woman, Gulnora, is caught carrying 27 bales of silk. What follows is far from routine. As the narrative unfolds, layers of corruption, secrets, and power games slowly come to light. The mysterious death of Customs Superintendent Ankit Tyagi—and the contrasting perspectives of his wife Poonam and Inspector Sandeep Yadav—adds depth and tension to the plot.

What truly stood out for me was how 'raw and realistic' the portrayal of government systems felt. The book doesn’t romanticise power or authority; instead, it shows how corruption, favours, and buried deals quietly operate behind closed doors. At times, it genuinely felt like watching a tightly edited, high-suspense thriller film play out scene by scene.

The characters are morally complex, especially Gulnora herself. Is she a victim of circumstances or a master manipulator? That question stays with you long after you turn the last page. The same goes for Prithvi, the enigmatic businessman whose presence adds an extra layer of intrigue.

The ending wasn’t something I could fully predict—and while it leaves several questions unanswered, it still worked for me. In fact, that ambiguity added to the overall impact, making the story linger in my mind.

If you’re looking for a 'fast-paced, gripping suspense thriller' that keeps you guessing and challenges your assumptions, *GulNora* is highly recommended. An absolute page-turner and a solid binge-read. 🔥

Title: A Song to Drown Rivers
Author: Ann Liang
Themes: power struggles; fragile alliances; war; identity; ambition
Tropes: rival kings; strategic alliances; personal sacrifice
Tags: Chinese author; historical fantasy; book club pick; translated fiction; under 300 pages; level:intermediate
Seasonal: Chinese New Year; Dragon Boat Festival
Collections: World Bookshelf; Civilizations Through Books; Civilization · China; Around the World in 52 Books; East Asia Shelf; Heartbreaking Reads; Comfort Reads; Dark & Atmospheric
One-line recommendation: A haunting and thought-provoking exploration of the human cost of war and the corrupting influence of power.
Personal notes:
Song to Drown Rivers was a beautifully written and deeply affecting read—but I’ll be honest, the ending broke my heart. I didn’t see it coming, and even after finishing the book, it stayed with me in a quiet, heavy way.

The novel does an excellent job of portraying the politics, power struggles, and fragile alliances between kingdoms. Every decision feels weighted, every move strategic, reminding us how personal lives often become casualties in larger political games. The writing is lyrical yet sharp, making the world feel both grand and painfully intimate.

What surprised me most was how my feelings shifted toward Fuchai, the rival king. By the end, I couldn’t bring myself to hate him. The moment where he asks Xishi to kill him rather than letting others do it was devastating—stripped of pride, power, and cruelty, leaving behind only a broken man. It was heartbreaking in a way I didn’t expect.

For me, the true villain of the story wasn’t the enemy king—it was Goujian. The brutality of his choices, especially the way he orchestrates Xishi’s fate, felt far more cruel than anything done in battle. Power, ambition, and vengeance completely overshadow humanity, and that realization hurt the most.

Somewhere deep inside, I was holding onto hope. I wanted Xishi and Fanli to finally have their peace, their long-deserved happy ending after the war. But the book chose realism over comfort—and that choice shattered me.

A Song to Drown Rivers is tragic, political, and emotionally intense. It’s not an easy read, but it’s a powerful one—especially if you’re okay with stories that don’t promise happy endings, only unforgettable ones.

Determined to uncover the truth, Inez travels to Cairo—only to find herself caught in a dangerous web of secrets, power struggles, and old-world magic.

A thoughtful and engaging continuation of the series.

Alchemised is one of those books that makes you understand why it’s so hyped, even if it tests your patience along the way. The story is long and sprawling, and I have to admit, there were moments in the first and third parts where I almost felt like giving up. The author’s attention to detail creates a universe that feels alive, with mysteries, politics, and magic interwoven into the characters’ journeys. The characters themselves are layered and compelling, and their arcs carry weight because you see their struggles, ambitions, and growth over time.

What I did find slightly disappointing was the ending. I was expecting something a bit more thrilling, more edge-of-the-seat, considering how gripping the middle sections were. While it wraps up the story, it didn’t hit me with the kind of high-stakes excitement I’d imagined. That said, the journey through the story is still engaging enough to make the long haul worth it.

Overall, Alchemised is a testament to why some books become sensations — it’s ambitious, immersive, and unforgettable. It’s the kind of story that demands patience but rewards readers with a rich, magical world and complex characters.

My take: A long, immersive read that’s worth it if you can push through the slower parts, even if the ending isn’t as thrilling as expected.

Their bond, though tested by time, separation, and betrayal, is the heart of the story, and watching them fight to protect each other is both thrilling and emotionally grounding.

Gunnhild’s journey from a determined, rebellious girl to a powerful witch is inspiring. Oddny’s grounded, loyal nature and Signy’s quiet strength balance her fire perfectly. Together, they navigate love, loss, revenge, and the brutal realities of Viking life. What I loved most was how the book didn’t just focus on battles or magic — it gave real depth to their choices, fears, and ambitions.

The world-building is incredible. The harsh, raw landscapes of Norway, the subtle weaving of Norse magic and prophecies, and the everyday life of the Viking era made me feel like I was right there with them, living every triumph and heartbreak. There’s tension, there’s emotion, and there’s an unexpected warmth that comes from the unbreakable bonds of friendship and loyalty.

Reading this book felt like getting lost in a legend that’s both epic and intimate. It’s smart, gripping, and utterly immersive. If you love historical fantasy with strong, nuanced female characters, magic woven into everyday life, and stories of loyalty and resilience, this one’s for you.

Both are wonderfully flawed, relatable characters whose choices, mistakes, and moments of vulnerability make them feel instantly real.
The narrative captures the messy, exhilarating, and sometimes bewildering aspects of modern life — from workplace politics to navigating romantic desires that refuse to stay casual. Meera’s impulsive attraction to a much younger colleague and Aalo’s flirtations with a distant war photographer highlight the awkward, funny, and sometimes heartbreaking ways we search for connection. Amid all this, the presence of a chosen family of loyal girlfriends adds warmth, humor, and grounding, reminding readers of the power of friendship.
What stands out most is how the book captures Mumbai itself — chaotic, unpredictable, and endlessly fascinating. The city becomes a character in its own right, shaping experiences, choices, and personal growth. Deepanjana Pal’s writing is sharp, witty, and evocative, turning even ordinary moments into poignant reflections on life and love.
Reading Lightning in a Shot Glass felt like stepping into a real-life version of 4 More Shots Please! — a story about women navigating uncertainty, self-discovery, and the pursuit of happiness in a world that constantly challenges them.
Verdict: A fun, smart, and emotionally resonant read that balances humor, romance, and introspection. Perfect for anyone who’s ever felt a little lost, a little confused, or in need of a story that celebrates friendship, love, and the magic of Mumbai.

Wuthering Heights is undoubtedly an influential classic, but it wasn't the reading experience I expected.

Going in, I had heard it described as one of the greatest romances ever written. However, I found the story to be much more focused on obsession, revenge, and emotional turmoil than romance.

The novel's atmosphere is powerful, and Emily Brontë's exploration of deeply flawed characters is impressive. However, I struggled to connect with most of the characters and often found their decisions frustrating.

Heathcliff, in particular, was difficult for me to view as a romantic figure, and I found myself sympathizing with very few people throughout the story.

While I can appreciate the book's literary significance and understand why it continues to be studied and discussed, it ultimately wasn't a personal favorite.

I would recommend it to readers interested in classic literature and Gothic fiction, but perhaps not to those looking for a traditional romance.

Ahmet Ümit beautifully blends Greek mythology, archaeology, history, and crime fiction to create an atmospheric thriller set around the ancient city of Pergamon. What I enjoyed the most was how the book introduced me to the historical and archaeological significance of Pergamon, especially the Altar of Zeus and the temples that once stood there.

I have always loved books that make me curious enough to explore the real-world history behind the story, and this one definitely did that.

The most interesting element for me was the narrative perspective of Zeus himself. It was an unusual choice, but it added a unique layer to the storytelling and created a fascinating connection between ancient myths and modern human struggles.

The book is also quite binge-worthy. The suspense, mystery, and constant discoveries kept me engaged throughout. The combination of mythology and investigation made it an interesting reading experience, especially for readers who enjoy historical mysteries.

After such a strong buildup filled with suspense, mythology, and historical depth, the conclusion felt a little abrupt and simpler than I expected. I was hoping for a more impactful payoff that matched the journey the book had taken me through.

That said, the ending does not take away from everything the book does well. The exploration of Pergamon, the archaeological details, and the unique storytelling approach made this a memorable read.

Would I recommend it?

Yes, especially if you enjoy Greek mythology, historical fiction, and archaeological mysteries.

But if you are picking this up expecting a thriller with an explosive climax and a shocking finale, it might leave you wanting more.

For me, The Land of Lost Gods was a fascinating journey through forgotten myths and ancient history—one that taught me something new while keeping me entertained.

Title: The Poet Empress
Author: Shen Tao
Themes: power struggles; politics; survival; fight for change; silencing voices; ambition; duty
Tags: Indian author; translated fiction; under 300 pages; book club pick; fantasy romance; historical fiction; strong female lead
Collections: India Bookshelf; Indian Historical Fiction; Civilizations Through Books; Civilization · China; Around the World in 52 Books; East Asia Shelf; Comfort Reads; Dark & Atmospheric
One-line recommendation: A beautifully written story about a woman who finds her voice in a world where women are forbidden from reading and writing.
Personal notes:
Some books catch your attention because of the story.
Some because of the characters.
And some because someone whose recommendations you trust makes you curious enough to pick them up.
I had been seeing The Poet Empress everywhere on Instagram, I knew I had to give it a try.
And I am glad I did.
What I expected was another fantasy novel.
What I got was a story deeply rooted in politics, power struggles, palace intrigue, survival, and the fight to change a system designed to silence certain voices.
What I loved most about this book was that it did not follow the usual fantasy romance path. Instead of focusing mainly on an enemy-to-lovers dynamic, Shen Tao builds a world where every relationship is influenced by power, ambition, duty, and the need to survive.
Wei Yin was easily the highlight of this story for me.
A simple rice farmer's daughter in a world where women are forbidden from reading and writing, she secretly learns the power of words. The journey of watching her discover knowledge, write poetry, and find her voice was incredibly powerful.
There was something beautiful about a woman who was never meant to hold power becoming someone who could change the entire course of a dynasty.
I also loved the contrast between the beauty of royalty and the darkness hidden behind palace walls. The luxury, the elegance, and the charm of the imperial world could not distract Wei Yin from making difficult choices when her country needed them most.
Terren was a complicated character for me.
I wouldn't say I hated him, but I couldn't completely like him either. His past and circumstances made me understand how he became the person he was. By the end, I did feel sympathy for him.
But I also understood Wei Yin's decision.
Sometimes personal feelings have to stand aside when a larger responsibility is involved. A country suffering from hunger needs stability and food, not another war.
One of my favourite aspects of the book was the role of poetry. The idea that words could hold such power, and that a poem could become something far more dangerous than simple writing, added a unique layer to the fantasy.
A few themes were difficult to read—especially how women were treated as tools for producing royal heirs and how education was deliberately kept away from them. But that also made Wei Yin's journey even more meaningful.
The Poet Empress is not just about royalty.
It is about a woman who was never given power, never given permission, and yet found a way to change everything.
A fast-paced fantasy with political games, unexpected turns, and a heroine who proves that sometimes the strongest weapon is a voice that refuses to be silenced.

Title: Ghachar Ghochar
Author: Vivek Shanbhag
Themes: family dynamics; power; money; human behavior; morality; comfort; relationships
Tags: Indian author; short read; book club pick; translated fiction; complex characters; level:intermediate
Collections: India Bookshelf; Indian Literary Fiction
One-line recommendation: A tiny but mighty book that will leave you questioning the characters' intentions and morality.
Personal notes:
We picked Ghachar Ghochar as our June book club read, and honestly… this tiny book did a complete ghachar ghochar of my mind.

(And yes, for those wondering, ghachar ghochar means something messy, tangled, or completely messed up—which is honestly the perfect word for this reading experience.)
This is a short read, but don't mistake its size for simplicity.


Vivek Shanbhag creates a story that looks ordinary on the surface but slowly reveals layers of family dynamics, power, money, and human behaviour. By the time you reach the end, you are left with so many questions—and interestingly, you can create your own interpretation of what really happened.

The characters are complex, mysterious, and honestly, quite questionable. Almost every person in this story makes choices that make you pause and wonder about their intentions.
The narrator especially frustrated me.

Among all the characters, he was the one I struggled with the most. His lack of courage and inability to take a stand made me question him throughout the story. He observes everything happening around him but rarely takes responsibility, which made him one of the most interesting yet frustrating characters.

What I loved about this book was how it explores the impact of money and comfort on people. It shows how circumstances can change relationships and how morality can become complicated when power enters the picture.

The ending is probably the biggest discussion point of the book. It does not give you clear answers. Instead, it leaves you sitting with your thoughts, creating your own understanding of what happened.

Would I reread this book?
Probably not.
Not because it wasn't good—but because one experience of this mental chaos is enough for me.

Would I recommend everyone to read it once?
Absolutely.

Ghachar Ghochar is messy, uncomfortable, thought-provoking, and unforgettable.
A small book that creates a very big conversation.

A woman with emotions, choices, strength, devotion, and her own journey.
What I loved most about this book was how it allowed me to know Rukmini closely. Mythological stories often focus on divine figures, but Saiswaroopa Iyer beautifully explores Krishna and Rukmini as human beings—with emotions, relationships, challenges, and vulnerabilities.

I personally believe female retellings bring a different kind of depth when written from a perspective that understands the complexities of a woman's experiences. And authors like Saiswaroopa Iyer continue to strengthen my belief in the importance of giving these women their own voices.

This book is not just a retelling of mythology.

Title: Dancing in the Mosque: An Afghan Mother's Letter to Her Son
Author: Homeira Qaderi
Themes: motherhood; suppression; education; choice; society; identity; culture
Tags: Afghan author; memoir; mother-son relationship; women's rights; book club pick; translated fiction
Collections: World Bookshelf; Middle East & North Africa; Around the World in 52 Books; Heartbreaking Reads; Comfort Reads
One-line recommendation: A powerful and heartbreaking memoir about motherhood, identity, and the suppression of women's rights.
Personal notes:
Some books are not just stories.
They are voices.
They are memories.

They are reminders of realities that many people around the world continue to experience.
Dancing in the Mosque: An Afghan Mother’s Letter to Her Son by Homeira Qaderi was one such book for me.

Those who know my reading journey know how much I love reading books about Afghanistan, especially stories that bring forward the experiences of women.
Yes, these books break my heart every time I read them.
But maybe that is the point.

Because sometimes the stories that hurt us the most are the ones that make us understand the most.

What made this book even more special was how deeply connected it feels to the author's own life. I am still not sure how much of this story mirrors her personal journey, but whatever parts come from reality, they carry a pain that feels incredibly honest.
This book is a mother's letter to her son, but it becomes much more than that.
It becomes a reflection of countless women whose voices have been suppressed.

Women who are denied education.
Women who are denied choices.

Women who are expected to exist only within roles decided by society.
One of the most heartbreaking parts of the book was the exploration of motherhood.
A woman carries a child for nine months, experiences unimaginable physical and emotional struggles, and brings a new life into the world.

Yet, even after giving so much of herself, her identity often remains secondary.
That thought stayed with me.
This book also made me reflect on how often restrictions on women are justified in the name of religion or tradition. But no belief system should be used to deny someone their basic human dignity, education, dreams, or freedom.

What I loved most is that despite all the pain, this book is not only about suffering.
It is about hope.
Hope that one day Afghan women will be able to study, work, dream, and live freely.
Hope that they will be seen not just as daughters, wives, or mothers—but as complete human beings.

Homeira Qaderi's voice is powerful because she transforms personal pain into a story that reaches beyond herself.

A heartbreaking, emotional, and important read.

Highly recommended.

One-line recommendation: A gripping historical fiction novel with a strong female protagonist and an engaging storyline.
Personal notes:
Indian historical fiction has always been one of my favourite genres.
There is something fascinating about travelling back in time through stories—exploring forgotten civilizations, ancient worlds, and imagining the lives of people who existed centuries ago.

Daughter of Two Rivers by Arun Krishnan had been sitting on my TBR for a long time.
And honestly, the title caught my attention first.
Then came the cover.

And yes, I admit it—I am someone who sometimes judges a book by its cover! 😅
But thankfully, the story lived up to the curiosity.
What I loved most about this book was Lilith, also known as Chitrangada.
Her warrior spirit, strength, and determination made her such an interesting protagonist. She carries the story with her fierce personality and makes you want to know what happens next.
Arjun's character was also enjoyable. He brings that classic gentleman hero energy—honourable, loyal, and supportive.

The biggest highlight for me was the historical setting.
The exploration of the Saraswati Valley civilization and the connection with the ancient city of Babylon added such an interesting layer to the story. The idea of lost civilizations, forgotten cities, and mysteries from the past immediately pulled me in.

Another thing I loved?The pacing.

This was the first paperback I finished in two days after a long time. The storytelling keeps moving, making it a perfect binge read for historical fiction lovers.
However, after finishing the book, I am still thinking about the title and its connection to the story. I am not completely sure I understood why this title was chosen.

And then came the ending.
Honestly?
It broke my heart.

After everything the characters went through—the struggles, challenges, and sacrifices—the conclusion was difficult to accept.
It was one of those endings where you just sit quietly and think:
"After everything… it had to end like this?"
Even now, I am still thinking about the possibility of such a massive earthquake changing the course of the Saraswati River and impacting an entire civilization. The idea itself is both fascinating and terrifying.

Overall, Daughter of Two Rivers is a captivating historical adventure filled with mystery, strong characters, and ancient-world imagination.

A 4.5-star read for me.
Highly recommended for anyone who loves Indian historical fiction, lost civilizations, and stories where history meets imagination.

Sometimes a book catches your attention because of its story.
Sometimes because of its title.
And sometimes… the cover is simply too beautiful to ignore.
The Vanishing Cherry Blossom Bookshop by Takuya Asakura was one of those books for me.
First of all, the cover is gorgeous.
And honestly, if a book has the word "book" in its title, I am already interested. 📚
This was a beautiful Japanese healing fiction that gave me exactly the kind of reading experience I was expecting—a warm, comforting, and emotional journey.
The first thing this book made me want to do?
Experience cherry blossom season in full bloom someday.
The way the story captures the beauty and emotion connected with cherry blossoms adds such a special charm. It creates a peaceful atmosphere that stays with you while reading.
But beyond the beautiful setting, this book is really about something much deeper.
It is about forgiveness.
Acceptance.
And learning to move forward without carrying the weight of guilt forever.
I loved how the story explores the idea that healing does not mean forgetting what happened. Sometimes healing means accepting your past and finding peace with it.
The book has a very feel-good quality. It is the kind of story you pick up when you need something gentle, emotional, and comforting.
However, the ending took me some time to fully understand. It was beautiful, but also slightly complicated, and I had to sit with it for a while before everything connected.
But once I understood the meaning behind it, I appreciated how it completed the emotional journey of the story.
Overall, The Vanishing Cherry Blossom Bookshop is a lovely Japanese fiction about healing, forgiveness, and finding hope after difficult moments.
A beautiful four-star read for me.
Perfect for anyone looking for a comforting story with books, emotions, and a little bit of cherry blossom magic. 🌸

One-line recommendation: A haunting and thought-provoking novel that explores the depths of human loneliness and the resilience of the human spirit in a post-apocalyptic world.
Personal notes:
I am honestly not sure what to say about this book.
Some stories are easy to review.
Some stories are not.
Because they do not just tell you a story—they leave you with questions.
I Who Have Never Known Men by Jacqueline Harpman was exactly that kind of book.
This book made me wonder:
What would I do if I was completely alone in the world?
No one to talk to.
No one to share memories with.
No one who understands what you are going through.
The thought itself is terrifying.
But imagine living your entire life like that.
Imagine never knowing what a normal world looks like because, as long as you remember, you have been trapped underground in a bunker.
A prisoner.
Surrounded only by women.
The only men you have ever known are prison guards.
Not fathers.
Not husbands.
Not partners.
Not friends.
Just guards.
That idea alone gave me chills.
The story follows a young girl who has lived with 39 other women in captivity. When they finally escape, instead of finding civilization, they discover an almost empty world.
And suddenly the questions become even bigger.
Are they still on Earth?
What happened to humanity?
Where did everyone go?
The most terrifying part of this book is not monsters or violence.
It is loneliness.
It is the idea of becoming a nomad in a world where everything familiar has disappeared.
Finding abandoned places.
Finding the remains of people who once existed.
Trying to understand a world you were never part of.
This is a short book, but the impact is massive.
It proves that a story does not need hundreds of pages to stay with you.
Throughout the book, I kept hoping we would finally discover:
Why were they imprisoned?
What exactly happened?
How did they reach this situation?
But the book ends with many mysteries still unanswered.
And surprisingly, that made the story even more haunting.
Because sometimes, not having answers is what makes a story unforgettable.
A spine-chilling, thought-provoking read that explores humanity, survival, and the need for connection.
Everyone should read this book at least once.
A 4.5-star read for me.
